questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is given an eye drop during an ophthalmology exam that stimulates cholinergic (parasympathetic) activity in the iris. Which of the following effects is most consistent with cholinergic activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decrease in gastric acid secretion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dilation of the bronchial smooth muscle

explanation.summary: Cholinergic (parasympathetic) activation drives 'rest and digest' effects, including pupillary constriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that cholinergic activation causes the iris to contract, producing pin-point (constricted) pupils. Parasympathetic tone promotes the rest-and-digest functions of the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation increases gastric secretions and acid production as part of digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic activation decreases heart rate through M2 receptors, rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergic activation increases bronchial contraction, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal-muscle vasodilation is not the cholinergic effect described; parasympathetic tone supports digestion and elimination.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A researcher studies a receptor that, when activated, triggers phospholipase C-beta to generate IP3 and DAG and raises intracellular calcium. Which of the following best describes this Gq-GPCR pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of cAMP production by adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of IP3 and calcium release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct opening of a ligand-gated sodium channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of cAMP through protein kinase A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the adenylyl cyclase enzyme

explanation.summary: The Gq pathway signals through IP3/DAG and calcium rather than through cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the Gq pathway differs from Gs and Gi because it involves calcium release and signaling via calcium-dependent pathways, activating IP3 and increasing cytosolic calcium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation of cAMP by adenylyl cyclase is the Gs (stimulatory) pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gq is a G-protein-coupled receptor pathway, not a ligand-gated ion channel like the nicotinic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting cAMP via protein kinase A describes the Gi pathway, not the calcium-based Gq pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase occurs with the Gi pathway, not Gq.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in septic shock is started on norepinephrine to raise his blood pressure. At therapeutic doses, norepinephrine has the greatest affinity for which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine acts primarily on alpha-1 receptors to raise blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states norepinephrine has more alpha-1 effects than alpha-2 or beta receptors (alpha-1 greater than alpha-2), causing constriction of vascular beds and increasing systemic vascular resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 receptors are only minimally affected by norepinephrine at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 receptors are less affected than alpha-1 at therapeutic doses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 receptors are minimally affected; norepinephrine is not selective for beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine is an adrenergic agonist and does not act on muscarinic cholinergic receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with decompensated heart failure and poor cardiac contractility is given dobutamine to improve her cardiac output. Dobutamine produces its positive inotropic effect mainly by stimulating which receptor?

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is a positive inotrope acting through beta-1 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dobutamine has high affinity for beta-1 receptors, and this beta-1 effect increases cardiac contractility (positive inotropic effect) as well as heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dobutamine does not have much alpha-2 effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-2 activity is mostly in the lungs and mediates bronchodilation, not the inotropic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-3 receptors are mostly in the urinary bladder and do not mediate inotropy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dopaminergic D1 receptors are targeted by dopamine in the renal vasculature, not by dobutamine.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is released by cholinergic neurons to mediate transmission?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic neurons release acetylcholine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines cholinergic neurons as those that release acetylcholine (ACh) to mediate transmission at the autonomic ganglia and at parasympathetic effector organs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dobutamine is a synthetic drug, not an endogenous neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine is not the neurotransmitter of cholinergic transmission described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla into the blood, an adrenergic signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine is released by adrenergic neurons, not cholinergic neurons.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: During a physiology demonstration, activation of a specific adrenergic receptor in the heart increases the heart rate. Which receptor is most responsible for this effect?

explanation.summary: Beta-1 receptors increase cardiac muscle contraction and heart rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states adrenergic beta-1 receptors are Gs-type GPCRs that increase cardiac muscle contraction and increase heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 receptors are mostly in the periphery and drive smooth-muscle (vascular) contraction, not heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and are not responsible for increasing heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 receptors mediate smooth-muscle relaxation and do not increase heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic M2 receptors decrease heart rate.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops anaphylaxis with wheezing and hypotension after a bee sting, and epinephrine is administered. Which receptor mediates the bronchodilation that helps relieve her wheezing?

explanation.summary: Epinephrine causes bronchodilation through beta-2 receptor activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that epinephrine has equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors and is helpful in bronchodilation through beta-2 activation in the lungs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 activation causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation increases cardiac contractility and heart rate rather than dilating bronchi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dopaminergic D2 receptors act in the renal vasculature and do not mediate bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic M3 activation causes bronchial constriction, the opposite effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A critically ill patient is started on dopamine. In addition to its cardiac effects, dopamine activates receptors in the renal vascular beds that produce local vasodilation. Which receptors mediate this renal effect?

explanation.summary: Dopamine acts on D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors in the renal vasculature to cause vasodilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dopamine activates D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors, which are in the renal vascular beds and produce vasodilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 activation (seen at higher dopamine doses) causes vasoconstriction, not the renal vasodilation described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation increases cardiac contractility rather than dilating renal vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic M2 receptors act on the heart to slow rate and are not the renal dopaminergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic nN receptors are ligand-gated channels at ganglia, not the renal vasodilatory receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with cardiogenic shock has poor cardiac contractility but is not profoundly vasodilated. The team wants an agent classified primarily as an inotrope to increase contractility rather than one used primarily as a vasopressor. Which agent best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is classified as an inotrope, whereas epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine are typically classified as vasopressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states dobutamine increases contractility (positive inotropic agent) and is therefore classified as an inotrope, in contrast to the agents grouped as vasopressors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dopamine is typically classified as a vasopressor in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine is typically classified as a vasopressor for its potent vascular effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is classified as a vasopressor with potent effects on the vasculature.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is a pure vasoconstrictor (pressor) and is not the inotrope described.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: All beta-adrenergic receptors couple to the same class of G protein. Activation of a beta receptor therefore leads to which of the following intracellular changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cAMP through Gi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased intracellular calcium through Gq inhibition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct sodium influx through a ligand-gated ion channel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased cAMP through Gs-mediated adenylyl cyclase activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased IP3 and DAG through Gq-mediated phospholipase C

explanation.summary: Beta receptors are Gs-coupled and raise cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that all beta receptors are Gs-type GPCRs, and the Gs (stimulatory) pathway activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased cAMP via Gi describes alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq signaling raises calcium; beta receptors do not act through Gq to lower calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct ion flux describes nicotinic ligand-gated channels, not GPCR-coupled beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased IP3/DAG via Gq describes alpha-1 and M3 receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A student is asked how nicotinic cholinergic receptors differ from the muscarinic and adrenergic receptors of the autonomic nervous system. Which of the following statements about nicotinic receptors is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are activated primarily by norepinephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are Gi-coupled GPCRs that lower cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are Gq-coupled GPCRs that raise intracellular calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are Gs-coupled GPCRs that raise cAMP

explanation.summary: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels opened by acetylcholine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick highlights that nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels activated by ACh, distinguishing them from the GPCR-based muscarinic and adrenergic receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nicotinic receptors are cholinergic and respond to acetylcholine, not norepinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gi-coupled cAMP inhibition describes alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not nicotinic channels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gq-coupled calcium signaling describes alpha-1 and M3 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gs-coupled cAMP signaling describes beta-adrenergic receptors, not nicotinic receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A patient in shock is given a vasopressor to restore blood pressure. Which mechanism best explains how a vasopressor raises blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased bronchial secretions through cholinergic activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced cardiac contractility that lowers cardiac output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slowing of the heart rate through M2 receptor activation

explanation.summary: Vasopressors raise blood pressure by increasing vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines vasopressors as agents that increase constriction of blood vessels; the resulting rise in vascular resistance increases blood pressure, which is useful in acute, hemodynamically unstable patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased bronchial secretions is a cholinergic effect unrelated to raising blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing contractility lowers cardiac output and would not raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slowing the heart rate is a cholinergic (M2) effect and does not describe vasopressor action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasodilation lowers vascular resistance and blood pressure, the opposite of a vasopressor effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is reviewing the functional divisions of the nervous system. The peripheral nervous system is divided into somatic and autonomic components. Which of the following is a division of the autonomic nervous system?

explanation.summary: The ANS is subdivided into the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and enteric nervous systems.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the peripheral nervous system is divided into the autonomic and somatic nervous systems, and the ANS is further divided into the parasympathetic nervous system (PSNS), sympathetic nervous system (SNS), and enteric nervous system (ENS).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The central nervous system is not part of the peripheral nervous system and is not a division of the ANS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endocrine system is not a division of the autonomic nervous system.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The peripheral nervous system is the parent division that contains the ANS, not one of its subdivisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The somatic nervous system is the other division of the peripheral nervous system, alongside the ANS, not a subdivision of it.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man begins sprinting on a treadmill. Within seconds his heart rate rises, his blood pressure rises, and his skeletal muscle metabolism increases simultaneously. Which feature of the sympathetic nervous system best explains why these changes occur together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It functions as a complete system with diffuse distribution through postganglionic fibers

choices.label: B
choices.text: It maintains homeostasis by regulating digestion and waste elimination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its ganglionic transmission is mediated by norepinephrine rather than acetylcholine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its neurotransmitters cross the lipid bilayer to act on intracellular receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its postganglionic neurons are unbranched and directed to a single organ

explanation.summary: The SNS functions as a complete system with diffuse postganglionic distribution, so multiple effector responses occur at once.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the SNS functions as a 'complete system,' with a diffused distribution through postganglionic fibers. It uses exercise as the example: heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle metabolism increase simultaneously, and the SNS prepares the body for any unknown situation requiring survival.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maintaining homeostasis through digestion and elimination is the role of the parasympathetic nervous system.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetylcholine, not norepinephrine, mediates transmission at the autonomic ganglia of both the SNS and PSNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neurotransmitters such as epinephrine are hydrophilic and have difficulty crossing the lipid bilayer; they act on cell surface receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unbranched postganglionic neurons directed to a specific organ describe the discrete parasympathetic output, not the diffuse sympathetic output.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is able to urinate without simultaneously defecating even though both processes are driven by parasympathetic activation. Which characteristic of the parasympathetic nervous system best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It discharges as a unit through widely branched postganglionic fibers

choices.label: B
choices.text: It prepares the body for unknown situations that may require survival responses

choices.label: C
choices.text: It releases epinephrine directly into the bloodstream to reach the effector organ

choices.label: D
choices.text: It uses norepinephrine as the neurotransmitter at the effector organ

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its innervations are direct and affect specific organs without discharging as a unit

explanation.summary: The PSNS does not discharge as a unit; its innervations are more direct and affect specific organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that the key distinction of the PSNS is that it does not discharge as a unit, using the example of how unpleasant a simultaneous urination and defecation response would be. In contrast to the SNS, PSNS innervations are more direct and affect specific organs, with postganglionic neurons that are not branched but directed to a specific organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Discharging as a unit through diffuse branched fibers describes the sympathetic nervous system.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Preparing the body for unknown threatening situations is the role of the sympathetic 'fight or flight' response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla into the bloodstream is a sympathetic feature, not a parasympathetic one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PSNS uses acetylcholine at the effector organ; norepinephrine is the sympathetic transmitter to effector organs.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: While hiking, a 33-year-old man unexpectedly encounters a bear. His heart races and his blood pressure rises. Which of the following best describes how epinephrine reaches his effector organs during this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Released at the autonomic ganglia to activate postganglionic neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Released by the adrenal medulla directly into the bloodstream

choices.label: C
choices.text: Released from parasympathetic postganglionic nerve terminals at the synapse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Released from sympathetic postganglionic fibers directly onto the heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesized locally within the smooth muscle cells of the effector organ

explanation.summary: Epinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla into the bloodstream to reach effector organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in emergency 'fight or flight' situations the adrenal medulla releases epinephrine (adrenaline) into the bloodstream, which promotes the responses at the effector organs. Epinephrine, released by the adrenal medulla, is released directly into the bloodstream to target the effector organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transmission at the autonomic ganglia is mediated by acetylcholine, not epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasympathetic postganglionic terminals release acetylcholine, not epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers mediate most transmission to effector organs with norepinephrine, not epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epinephrine is not synthesized within the effector organ; it arrives via the bloodstream from the adrenal medulla.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A pharmacologist studies transmission from sympathetic postganglionic fibers to vascular smooth muscle. Which neurotransmitter mediates most of this neurotransmission to the effector organ?

explanation.summary: In the SNS, norepinephrine mediates most neurotransmission to the effector organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that when norepinephrine or epinephrine is the neurotransmitter, the fiber is adrenergic, and that in the SNS norepinephrine mediates most neurotransmission to the effector organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine is released at the autonomic ganglia of both divisions and by parasympathetic postganglionic nerves, not by sympathetic fibers to vascular smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dobutamine is a synthetic beta-1 agonist drug, not an endogenous neurotransmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine is discussed in the brick as a sympathomimetic drug, not as the transmitter released by sympathetic postganglionic fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoproterenol is a synthetic beta-agonist drug, not an endogenous neurotransmitter.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: An experimental agent blocks neurotransmission at the autonomic ganglia, and both sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow to effector organs are reduced. Which of the following neurotransmitters and release sites is most likely being antagonized?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetylcholine, released at ganglia of both divisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetylcholine, released at ganglia of the parasympathetic division only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epinephrine, released at ganglia of both divisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Norepinephrine, released at ganglia of both divisions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Norepinephrine, released at ganglia of the sympathetic division only

explanation.summary: Acetylcholine is released at the autonomic ganglia in both the SNS and the PSNS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the release of ACh occurs at the autonomic ganglia in both the SNS and PSNS. Blocking ganglionic transmission would therefore reduce outflow from both divisions, consistent with antagonism of acetylcholine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetylcholine is the ganglionic transmitter in both divisions, not the parasympathetic division alone, which is why both outflows are reduced.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla into the bloodstream; it is not the ganglionic transmitter.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is not the ganglionic transmitter of either division.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine mediates sympathetic transmission to effector organs, not transmission at the ganglia.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A researcher notes that epinephrine and acetylcholine must bind receptors on the cell surface and rely on second messengers to produce a cellular response. Which property of these neurotransmitters best explains this requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are hydrophilic and cross the lipid bilayer poorly

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are lipophilic and diffuse freely through the membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are rapidly degraded in the extracellular space

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are too large to bind any membrane receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: They bind directly to nuclear transcription factors

explanation.summary: Epinephrine and ACh are hydrophilic, so they act on cell surface receptors and second messengers propagate the response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that neurotransmitters such as epinephrine and ACh are hydrophilic and have a difficult time crossing the lipid bilayer. They therefore relay the stimulus by activating cell surface receptors (signal detector and transducer), and second messengers further propagate the response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These neurotransmitters are hydrophilic, not lipophilic, and do not diffuse freely across the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extracellular degradation is not the reason given for surface receptor signaling; the barrier is the lipid bilayer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neurotransmitters do bind membrane receptors; that is precisely how they signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Because they cannot readily cross the lipid bilayer, they do not act directly on nuclear factors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A drug selectively activates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors. Which of the following intracellular changes is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cAMP through inhibition of adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased calcium binding to calmodulin in cardiac muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased cAMP through stimulation of adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased IP3 and calcium release through phospholipase C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opening of a ligand-gated ion channel

explanation.summary: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled, and the Gi pathway inhibits cAMP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's adrenergic receptor figure assigns alpha-2 to Gi. The Gi (G-inhibitory) pathway inhibits production of the messenger molecule cAMP, the opposite of Gs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium binding to calmodulin describes inotropy in cardiac cells, not the alpha-2 signaling pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased cAMP via adenylyl cyclase is the Gs pathway, used by beta receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IP3 and calcium release is the Gq pathway, used by alpha-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ligand-gated ion channels are the nicotinic receptors, not alpha-2 GPCRs.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man's heart rate falls after a cholinergic agonist is administered. Which receptor and G-protein class mediate this effect?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation decreases heart rate through Gi-coupled M2 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's cholinergic receptor figure assigns M2 to Gi, and highlights that M2 and M3 are important to remember because they work in the heart and lungs. Cholinergic activation decreases heart rate by activation of M2 receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-1 is an adrenergic Gs receptor that increases heart rate, and it is not activated by a cholinergic agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M1 is Gq-coupled and is not the cardiac muscarinic receptor that lowers heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 is an adrenergic Gi receptor, not a cholinergic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M3 is Gq-coupled and mediates effects in the lungs such as bronchial contraction, not slowing of the heart.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman develops bronchial smooth muscle contraction after exposure to a cholinergic agonist. Which receptor and second-messenger pathway most likely mediate this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptor signaling through decreased cAMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-2 receptor signaling through increased cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: M2 receptor signaling through decreased cAMP

choices.label: D
choices.text: M3 receptor signaling through IP3 and calcium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic nM receptor acting as a ligand-gated channel

explanation.summary: M3 receptors in the lungs are Gq-coupled and mediate cholinergic bronchial contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick assigns M3 to Gq, which signals through IP3 and calcium release, and highlights M3 as working in the lungs. Cholinergic activation increases bronchial contraction, the opposite of adrenergic beta-2 relaxation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-2 is an adrenergic receptor and is not activated by a cholinergic agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-2 activation causes smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation, not contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M2 is the Gi-coupled cardiac muscarinic receptor that decreases heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The nicotinic nM receptor is the muscle-type nicotinic channel, not the muscarinic receptor of bronchial smooth muscle.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is assigning each cholinergic receptor subtype to its signaling mechanism. Which of the following receptors is coupled to Gi?

explanation.summary: M2 and M4 are Gi-coupled; M1, M3, and M5 are Gq-coupled; no muscarinic receptor is Gs-coupled.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's cholinergic receptor figure lists M1 Gq, M2 Gi, M3 Gq, M4 Gi, and M5 Gq, and highlights that there is no muscarinic receptor that is a Gs-type GPCR. M4 is therefore the Gi-coupled receptor among the choices.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M1 is Gq-coupled.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M3 is Gq-coupled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M5 is Gq-coupled.
whyWrongByChoice.E: nN is a neuronal nicotinic receptor, a ligand-gated channel rather than a G-protein coupled receptor.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes a nicotinic cholinergic receptor located on skeletal muscle. Which of the following subtypes is this?

explanation.summary: Nicotinic receptors are divided into nM (muscle) and nN (neuron) subtypes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's classification of cholinergic receptors divides nicotinic receptors into nM (Muscle) and nN (Neuron). A nicotinic receptor on skeletal muscle is the nM subtype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M2 is a muscarinic GPCR (Gi), not a nicotinic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M3 is a muscarinic GPCR (Gq), not a nicotinic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M5 is a muscarinic GPCR (Gq), not a nicotinic receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: nN is the neuronal nicotinic subtype, not the muscle subtype.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Two autonomic receptors, one adrenergic and one cholinergic, both signal through Gq-mediated calcium release. Which of the following pairs is correct?

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 (all subtypes) and M1, M3, M5 are the Gq-coupled autonomic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick highlights that all alpha-1 receptor subtypes are Gq-type GPCRs, and its cholinergic figure assigns M3 to Gq. Both signal through calcium release and calcium-dependent pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 is Gs-coupled; only M1 is Gq.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 and M2 are both Gi-coupled, inhibiting cAMP production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 is Gs-coupled and M4 is Gi-coupled; neither is Gq.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-3 is Gs-coupled and M2 is Gi-coupled; neither is Gq.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man receives a therapeutic dose of epinephrine. His systolic blood pressure rises, but his diastolic blood pressure falls slightly. Which effect of epinephrine best explains the fall in diastolic pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 mediated constriction of vascular beds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-1 mediated increase in heart rate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-2 mediated bronchodilation in the lungs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gi-mediated inhibition of cAMP in the heart

explanation.summary: Epinephrine dilates skeletal muscle vascular beds, so diastolic blood pressure might fall even as systolic rises.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that epinephrine increases systolic blood pressure through alpha-1 vasoconstriction of vascular beds, but in the skeletal muscle epinephrine induces vasodilation, hence diastolic blood pressure might fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction is what raises the systolic blood pressure, not what lowers the diastolic pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation raises heart rate, contractility, stroke volume, and cardiac output; it does not lower diastolic pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bronchodilation is a pulmonary effect and does not account for a change in diastolic blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine acts on alpha and beta receptors; Gi-mediated cAMP inhibition in the heart is a muscarinic M2 effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman in shock is started on a therapeutic infusion of norepinephrine. Unlike a patient receiving epinephrine, whose diastolic pressure might fall, she has a rise in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Which property of norepinephrine best explains this hemodynamic pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of D1 and D2 receptors in the kidneys

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Predominant alpha-1 activity constricting all vascular beds

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selective activation of beta-2 receptors in the lungs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation of skeletal muscle vascular beds

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine's alpha-1 predominance constricts all vascular beds, raising both systolic and diastolic pressure and SVR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that norepinephrine has more alpha-1 effects than alpha-2 or beta receptors (alpha-1 >> alpha-2), which causes constriction of all vascular beds. This allows it to increase blood pressure (systolic and diastolic) and the systemic vascular resistance, in contrast to epinephrine, which induces skeletal muscle vasodilation that may lower diastolic pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: D1 and D2 activation in the renal vascular beds is a dopamine effect that produces vasodilation, not a pressure rise.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors describes epinephrine, not norepinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is non-selective for beta receptor activation and does not selectively activate beta-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle vasodilation is an epinephrine effect that lowers diastolic pressure; norepinephrine constricts all vascular beds.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is in cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. High-quality CPR is in progress and epinephrine is to be given according to ACLS protocol. Which of the following is the appropriate epinephrine dosing?

choices.label: E
choices.text: 10 mg intravenously as a single dose

explanation.summary: In ACLS resuscitation, epinephrine is given as 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical reasoning box states that epinephrine, a cornerstone of ACLS protocols, is administered in 1 mg doses intravenously every 3-5 minutes during resuscitation efforts, and is crucial for managing arrhythmias such as asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.1 mg every 10 minutes is neither the dose nor the interval described for resuscitation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.3 mg every minute is not the described dose or interval.
whyWrongByChoice.C: During resuscitation, epinephrine is given intravenously, not intramuscularly every 15 minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single 10 mg dose is not the ACLS regimen; epinephrine is given in repeated 1 mg doses.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: During CPR for a 65-year-old man found pulseless and barely breathing, epinephrine is administered. Which effect of epinephrine is primarily responsible for improving blood flow to the heart and brain during resuscitation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction raising vascular resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: D1 and D2 mediated vasodilation of the renal vascular beds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-2 mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase in nerve terminals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-2 mediated relaxation of the bronchial smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: M2 mediated decrease in heart rate and conduction velocity

explanation.summary: Epinephrine's vasoconstriction improves blood flow to vital organs, particularly the heart and brain, during CPR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that epinephrine's alpha-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation causes vasoconstriction, increasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure, and that this vasoconstriction helps improve blood flow to vital organs, particularly the heart and brain, during cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal vasodilation via D1 and D2 receptors is an effect of dopamine, not epinephrine, and does not improve coronary or cerebral flow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 Gi signaling is not the mechanism cited for improved vital organ perfusion during CPR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bronchodilation is a pulmonary effect of epinephrine and does not redirect blood flow to the heart and brain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M2-mediated slowing of the heart is a cholinergic effect, not an epinephrine effect.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is found in asystole, with no electrical or mechanical activity of the heart. After two doses of epinephrine during CPR, a heart rhythm is detected. Which action of epinephrine most directly addresses the absence of cardiac electrical activity?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta stimulation enhancing cardiac electrical activity

explanation.summary: Beta-adrenergic stimulation by epinephrine enhances the electrical activity of the heart, which is crucial in asystole.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case conclusion explains that beta-adrenergic stimulation by epinephrine increases heart rate and contractility, can help restart the heart, and additionally can enhance the electrical activity of the heart, which is crucial in cases of asystole where there is no detectable electrical activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises SVR and improves flow to the heart and brain, but it does not directly restore electrical activity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-2 Gi signaling inhibits cAMP and is not the action that enhances cardiac electrical activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bronchodilation is a pulmonary effect unrelated to cardiac electrical activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal vasodilation via dopaminergic receptors is a dopamine effect, not the mechanism by which epinephrine addresses asystole.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with hypotension is receiving dopamine, which initially improves his cardiac contractility. As the dose is escalated, marked vasoconstriction and a sharp rise in blood pressure develop. Which receptor effect best explains the change at higher doses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased alpha-1 activation in vascular beds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased beta-2 activation in bronchial smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased D1 receptor activation in renal vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased M3 activation in vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of beta-1 activation in the heart

explanation.summary: Dopamine activates beta-1 at therapeutic doses, and higher doses add alpha-1 effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that at therapeutic doses dopamine activates beta-1 and increases cardiac contractility, and that higher doses can also increase alpha-1 effects. Alpha-1 activation constricts vascular beds and raises blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-2 activation relaxes smooth muscle and would not cause vasoconstriction or a pressure spike.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D1 activation in the renal vascular beds produces vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 is a cholinergic receptor and is not activated by dopamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-1 activation is the therapeutic-dose effect and is not lost at higher doses; alpha-1 effects are added.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman receives isoproterenol during a hemodynamic study. Her heart rate and contractility increase and her bronchial smooth muscle relaxes. Which receptor profile best describes this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equal activation of alpha and beta receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Equal activation of beta-1 and beta-2 receptors

explanation.summary: Isoproterenol is a potent activator of both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors (beta-1 = beta-2).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes isoproterenol as a potent activator of both beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors (beta-1 = beta-2). It increases heart rate and cardiac contractility and causes bronchodilation by beta-2 activation (relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle).

whyWrongByChoice.A: D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptor activation describes dopamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors describes epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Greater alpha-1 than alpha-2 activation describes norepinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Greater beta-1 than beta-2 affinity describes dobutamine, not isoproterenol.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A critical care team is comparing dobutamine and isoproterenol for a patient whose main problem is poor cardiac contractility. Which statement correctly contrasts the two agents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dobutamine dilates bronchial smooth muscle more than isoproterenol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dobutamine is a vasopressor whereas isoproterenol is an inotrope

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isoproterenol acts mainly through alpha-1 receptors, unlike dobutamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isoproterenol binds beta-1 more strongly than beta-2 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isoproterenol raises cardiac output and heart rate less than dobutamine

explanation.summary: Isoproterenol's increases in cardiac output and heart rate are less than those of dobutamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that with isoproterenol, cardiac output and heart rate increase; however, these effects are less compared to dobutamine. Dobutamine has high affinity for beta-1 receptors and its beta-1 effect raises heart rate, stroke volume, and cardiac output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchodilation through beta-2 activation is described for isoproterenol, not dobutamine, which favors beta-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dobutamine is classified as an inotrope (positive inotropic agent), not a vasopressor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isoproterenol is a beta-1 and beta-2 activator, not an alpha-1 agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoproterenol activates beta-1 and beta-2 equally; it is dobutamine that has higher affinity for beta-1 than beta-2.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A synthetic derivative of an endogenous adrenergic neurotransmitter activates adrenergic receptors and reproduces responses of the sympathetic nervous system. Which term best describes this agent?

explanation.summary: Adrenergic agonists that mimic the SNS are called sympathomimetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that synthesized neurotransmitters or their derivatives are autonomic agents, also known as adrenergic or cholinergic agonists. Agonists that activate adrenergic receptors mimic the sympathetic nervous system and are therefore called sympathomimetics (sympatho = SNS, mimetics = mimicking the sympathetic system).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cholinergic agonist activates cholinergic (ACh) receptors, not adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A ganglionic blocker inhibits transmission at autonomic ganglia rather than activating adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A muscarinic antagonist blocks receptors rather than activating them and targets cholinergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A parasympathomimetic would mimic the parasympathetic system, not the sympathetic system.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A positive inotropic agent raises intracellular calcium in cardiac cells, increasing the force of contraction. Calcium produces this effect by binding to which of the following?

explanation.summary: Inotropy reflects intracellular calcium binding to calmodulin, which increases cardiac muscle contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the 'ion' of inotropy refers to calcium: when intracellular calcium increases, it binds to calmodulin, which increases muscle contraction. In cardiac cells this increases the force of cardiac contractility, and agents that increase contractility are positive inotropic agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenylyl cyclase generates cAMP in the Gs pathway; it is not the calcium-binding protein of inotropy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IP3 is a second messenger that triggers calcium release; it is not what calcium binds to increase contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C generates IP3 and DAG in the Gq pathway; it is not the target of calcium described for inotropy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein kinase A is a downstream effector of cAMP, not the protein calcium binds to increase contraction.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A drug selectively activates beta-3 adrenergic receptors. Based on where these receptors are mostly expressed, which organ is the primary target?

explanation.summary: Beta-3 receptors are mostly expressed in the urinary bladder and have no inotropic function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that beta-3 receptors are mostly expressed in the urinary bladder and do not have any inotropic functions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The heart is the site of beta-1 (and M2) receptors, which govern rate and contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The iris responds to cholinergic activation with contraction (pin-point pupils), not beta-3 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The renal vascular beds express D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors that mediate vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lungs are the site of beta-2 (and M3) receptors, which govern bronchial smooth muscle tone.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is found unresponsive and pulseless. EMS begins high-quality CPR and administers epinephrine intravenously during the resuscitation. Which of the following best explains the pharmacologic rationale for giving epinephrine during cardiac arrest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates alpha-1 receptors only, with no effect on the myocardium

choices.label: B
choices.text: It activates both alpha and beta adrenergic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: It activates dopaminergic D1 receptors to dilate renal vascular beds

choices.label: D
choices.text: It blocks muscarinic M2 receptors to increase heart rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: It selectively activates beta-2 receptors to produce bronchodilation

explanation.summary: Epinephrine has roughly equal affinity for alpha and beta receptors, which is why it is the cornerstone drug in cardiac arrest.
explanation.whyCorrect: Epinephrine stimulates alpha-1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction, increasing systemic vascular resistance and improving perfusion pressure to the heart and brain. It simultaneously stimulates beta-1 receptors to increase heart rate and myocardial contractility, helping to restore effective circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta receptors and has prominent beta-1 mediated cardiac effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopaminergic D1 renal vasodilation is a property of dopamine, not epinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine is an adrenergic agonist, not a muscarinic antagonist; it does not block M2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-2 bronchodilation is one action of epinephrine but is not the rationale for its use in arrest, and epinephrine is not beta-2 selective.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with septic shock remains hypotensive despite fluids. She is started on a vasopressor that constricts all vascular beds and raises both systolic and diastolic blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance, with only weak beta activity. Which receptor does this agent target most strongly?

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine has greater affinity for alpha-1 than alpha-2 or beta receptors, producing widespread vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: At therapeutic doses norepinephrine acts predominantly on alpha-1 receptors (alpha-1 much greater than alpha-2), constricting all vascular beds. This raises systolic and diastolic blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance, which is why it is used as a vasopressor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation would increase contractility and rate, but the described effect is vascular tone; norepinephrine is not primarily beta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine has more alpha-1 than alpha-2 effect; alpha-2 is not the primary target driving vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2 activation causes vasodilation and bronchodilation, the opposite of the vasoconstriction described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M2 is a cholinergic receptor that slows the heart and is unrelated to adrenergic vasoconstriction.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with acute decompensated heart failure has a low cardiac output but adequate blood pressure. The team wants an agent that predominantly increases myocardial contractility through beta-1 receptors (with high beta-1 relative to beta-2 selectivity) and minimal pressor effect. Which agent best fits this profile?

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is a beta-1 selective positive inotropic agent used to raise contractility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dobutamine has higher affinity for beta-1 than beta-2 receptors. This beta-1 mediated effect increases cardiac contractility (positive inotropy) and heart rate, raising stroke volume and cardiac output, so it is classified as an inotrope rather than a vasopressor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dopamine activates beta-1 but also dopaminergic and (at higher doses) alpha-1 receptors, and is classified as a vasopressor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta receptors, giving it prominent vasopressor activity rather than selective inotropy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoproterenol activates beta-1 and beta-2 equally and is non-selective, not beta-1 selective.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine acts mainly on alpha-1 to raise vascular resistance and is used as a vasopressor, not a selective beta-1 inotrope.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A sympathomimetic is given at therapeutic doses to a critically ill patient. In addition to activating beta-1 receptors to increase cardiac contractility, it activates D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors in the renal vascular beds to produce vasodilation. Which agent is being described?

explanation.summary: Dopamine uniquely activates dopaminergic D1 and D2 receptors in addition to adrenergic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: At therapeutic doses dopamine activates beta-1 receptors to increase contractility, and higher doses increase alpha-1 effects. It also activates D1 and D2 dopaminergic receptors located in the renal vascular beds, producing renal vasodilation, a property unique to dopamine among these agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dobutamine acts on beta-1 receptors and does not activate dopaminergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epinephrine acts on alpha and beta receptors but not dopaminergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isoproterenol is a non-selective beta agonist without dopaminergic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine acts predominantly on alpha-1 and has no dopaminergic action.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A drug is described as a potent activator of both beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors (beta-1 equals beta-2) with no alpha activity. It increases heart rate and contractility and also causes bronchodilation by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Which agent is this?

explanation.summary: Isoproterenol is a non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 agonist.
explanation.whyCorrect: Isoproterenol activates beta-1 and beta-2 receptors equally. Beta-1 activation increases heart rate and contractility (though less than dobutamine), and beta-2 activation causes bronchodilation by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. It has no alpha activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dobutamine is beta-1 selective (beta-1 greater than beta-2), not an equal beta-1/beta-2 agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dopamine acts on beta-1, dopaminergic, and alpha-1 receptors rather than being a pure non-selective beta agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is predominantly an alpha-1 agonist and is non-selective for beta, not an equal beta-1/beta-2 activator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist and would not cause bronchodilation or tachycardia.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Norepinephrine binds alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction. Which intracellular signaling change is produced by activation of this G-protein-coupled receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cAMP through a Gi pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct opening of a ligand-gated sodium channel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased cAMP through a Gs pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased IP3, DAG and intracellular Ca2+

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 receptors are Gq-coupled and signal through the phospholipase C / IP3 / Ca2+ cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: All alpha-1 receptor subtypes are Gq-type GPCRs. Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP2 into IP3 and DAG and raises intracellular Ca2+. The rise in Ca2+ drives smooth muscle contraction and vasoconstriction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased cAMP via Gi is the mechanism of alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not alpha-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ligand-gated ion channel opening describes nicotinic receptors, not GPCR-linked alpha-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased cAMP via Gs is the mechanism of beta receptors, not alpha-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cGMP pathway is not the second messenger system used by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Epinephrine increases heart rate and contractility by activating beta-1 receptors in the myocardium. Which G protein and second messenger mediate this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ligand-gated cation channel with direct depolarization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gq, with increased intracellular Ca2+ only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gq, with increased IP3 and DAG

explanation.summary: All beta receptors are Gs-coupled and act by raising cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beta-1 receptors are Gs-type GPCRs. Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and activating protein kinase A, which enhances cardiac contractility and heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ligand-gated cation channels describe nicotinic receptors, not beta-1 GPCRs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gi with decreased cAMP is the pathway of alpha-2 and M2 receptors, which slow the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-1 signaling works through Gs and cAMP, not a Gq/Ca2+ mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gq with IP3 and DAG is the pathway of alpha-1 and M1/M3/M5 receptors, not beta-1.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Increased parasympathetic (cholinergic) tone slows the heart. Activation of which receptor is responsible for decreasing heart rate?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic slowing of the heart is mediated by the Gi-coupled M2 muscarinic receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cholinergic activation decreases heart rate by activating M2 receptors, which are Gi-coupled GPCRs important in the heart. This opposes the sympathetic beta-1 effect in the constant tug-of-war between the two systems.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 receptors mediate vasoconstriction, not slowing of the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-1 activation increases, rather than decreases, heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors act on glandular and smooth muscle (for example bronchial contraction), not the pacemaker slowing described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels at ganglia and muscle, not the cardiac rate-slowing receptor.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to identify a physiologic response that results from cholinergic (parasympathetic) activation. Which of the following is the best example?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation produces rest-and-digest effects such as pupillary constriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cholinergic (parasympathetic) activation contracts the iris, producing pin-point pupils (miosis). This is a classic rest-and-digest response mediated by muscarinic receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation causes bronchoconstriction; bronchodilation is a sympathetic beta-2 effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholinergic activation increases gastric acid secretion; a decrease is not a parasympathetic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased contractility is a sympathetic (beta-1) effect, not cholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasoconstriction is a sympathetic alpha-1 effect, not a cholinergic response.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: Unlike muscarinic and adrenergic receptors, which are G-protein-coupled receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors transmit their signal by a different mechanism. Which of the following best describes the nicotinic receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Gi-coupled receptor that lowers cAMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Gq-coupled receptor that raises intracellular Ca2+ via IP3

choices.label: C
choices.text: A Gs-coupled receptor that raises cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: A voltage-gated calcium channel independent of acetylcholine

explanation.summary: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels, not GPCRs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated channels that are opened directly by acetylcholine, allowing cation influx and direct depolarization without using a G protein or second messenger.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gi-coupled lowering of cAMP describes alpha-2 and M2 receptors, not nicotinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq-coupled IP3/Ca2+ signaling describes alpha-1 and certain muscarinic receptors, not nicotinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gs-coupled cAMP signaling describes beta adrenergic receptors, not nicotinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic channels are ligand-gated (opened by ACh), not voltage-gated calcium channels.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A hemodynamically unstable patient needs support to restore contractility. The team selects an agent that increases cardiac contractility and cardiac output and is classified as a positive inotropic agent (inotrope) rather than a vasopressor. Which of the following agents fits this classification?

explanation.summary: Dobutamine is classified as a positive inotropic agent; epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine are classified as vasopressors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dobutamine increases contractility (inotropy) and cardiac output through its beta-1 effect, and in practice is classified as an inotrope or positive inotropic agent used to restore hemodynamic stability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine is the endogenous cholinergic neurotransmitter, not a vasopressor or inotrope used in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopamine has potent effects on the vasculature and is classified as a vasopressor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epinephrine has potent vascular effects and is classified as a vasopressor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norepinephrine acts mainly on the vasculature and is classified as a vasopressor.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: The term inotropy refers to a change in cardiac contractility. In a positive inotropic response, an increase in the intracellular concentration of a specific ion binds calmodulin and increases the force of cardiac muscle contraction. Which ion is responsible for this effect?

explanation.summary: Inotropy depends on intracellular calcium, which binds calmodulin to increase contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ion of inotropy is Ca2+. When intracellular Ca2+ increases, it binds calmodulin, which increases muscle contraction; in cardiac cells this raises the force of contractility, defining a positive inotropic effect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chloride is not the ion described as binding calmodulin to increase contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Magnesium is not the ion responsible for the inotropic increase in cardiac contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium governs repolarization and resting potential, not the calmodulin-mediated increase in contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sodium influx contributes to depolarization but is not the ion that binds calmodulin to drive contractility.

questions.topicName: Autonomic Nervous System - Vasopressors and Inotropes

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is started on clonidine. Which of the following best explains how this drug lowers his blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals

choices.label: D
choices.text: It raises cAMP in cardiac myocytes to slow the heart

explanation.summary: Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-2 receptors sit on the terminals of presynaptic sympathetic neurons in the brain. When clonidine activates them, norepinephrine release is decreased, reducing activation of CNS adrenergic receptors and lowering blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist, not an alpha-1 blocker; it does not act as an antagonist on vascular smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonidine decreases, not increases, norepinephrine release; increasing release would raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ACE inhibition is a separate drug class and is not the mechanism of clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled and lower cAMP; clonidine does not raise cardiac cAMP.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman in the intensive care unit is given intravenous phenylephrine to treat hypotension. Shortly afterward her heart rate slows. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct alpha-1 stimulation of the sinoatrial node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased norepinephrine release in the brainstem

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia from arterial baroreceptor unloading

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 agonist-induced rises in systemic vascular resistance trigger reflex bradycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylephrine increases alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance. This activates the baroreceptor reflex, causing a decrease in sympathetic outflow and therefore a fall in heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist and does not block cardiac beta-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heart-rate change is a baroreceptor reflex, not direct alpha-1 action on the SA node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine acts peripherally on vasculature; it does not increase brainstem norepinephrine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rising blood pressure loads, rather than unloads, the baroreceptors, and the reflex slows rather than speeds the heart.

questions.stem: Phenylephrine binds alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle. Which of the following intracellular signaling sequences most directly produces the resulting contraction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of guanylyl cyclase increasing cGMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct opening of voltage-gated potassium channels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gi activation decreases adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gs activation increases adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 receptors are Gq-coupled and signal through the PLC/IP3/calcium pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alpha-1 receptor is a Gq-type GPCR. Activation stimulates phospholipase C, which converts PIP2 to IP3. IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, raising cytosolic calcium and driving smooth muscle contraction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cGMP signaling promotes vasodilation and is unrelated to alpha-1 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opening potassium channels would hyperpolarize and relax, not contract, the muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gi-mediated lowering of cAMP is the alpha-2 pathway, not the alpha-1 contraction mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gs/cAMP signaling is not the alpha-1 pathway and would not drive this contraction.

questions.stem: A patient uses an intranasal phenylephrine spray for congestion. Which of the following best describes how the drug relieves the congestion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of histamine receptors in the nasal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of mucus-secreting glands via muscarinic blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stimulation of beta-2 receptors relaxing airway smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasodilation that flushes secretions from the sinuses

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine decongests by alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction of nasal vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Direct stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the nasal mucosa causes vasoconstriction of local nasal vessels. This decreases mucosal edema, producing the decongestant effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It is an alpha-1 agonist, not an antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not work through muscarinic blockade of glands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine is selective for alpha-1 receptors, not beta-2 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation, and its effect is on vessel tone, not flushing.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant develops hypertension that requires pharmacologic treatment. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Methyldopa is the alpha-2 agonist indicated for hypertension in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyldopa can be used for all types of hypertension and is specifically indicated during pregnancy, where it is useful for patients who develop adverse effects or become intolerant to other commonly used medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an antihypertensive but is not the agent specifically indicated during pregnancy in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine is a vasopressor that raises blood pressure and would be inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-1 agonist for decongestion and eye redness, not for hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that raises blood pressure and would worsen hypertension.

questions.stem: Methyldopa is often called a false neurotransmitter. Which of the following best explains this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It competitively antagonizes norepinephrine at postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: It depletes dopamine stores in the substantia nigra, which reduces central sympathetic outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases synthesis of norepinephrine from tyrosine by activating tyrosine hydroxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: It irreversibly blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the synapse by inhibiting the NET transporter

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, which is released in place of norepinephrine

explanation.summary: Methyldopa is converted to a selective alpha-2 agonist that substitutes for norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methyldopa is taken up into sympathetic nerve terminals and metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a selective alpha-2 agonist. This metabolite is loaded into presynaptic vesicles and released in place of norepinephrine, so activating presynaptic alpha-2 receptors decreases sympathetic outflow and lowers blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: It acts as an alpha-2 agonist through its metabolite, not as an alpha-1 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Its antihypertensive action involves sympathetic terminals, not dopamine depletion in the substantia nigra.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It substitutes for norepinephrine rather than increasing norepinephrine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyldopa is not a reuptake inhibitor; it is stored and released as a false transmitter.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man taking clonidine for hypertension reports a persistently dry mouth. Which of the following terms best describes this adverse effect?

explanation.summary: Dry mouth from clonidine is called xerostomia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Xerostomia, or dryness of the mouth, is a common adverse effect associated with clonidine use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extravasation refers to a drug leaking into tissue at an IV site, not to dry mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypersalivation is the opposite of the dry mouth seen with clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mydriasis is pupil dilation, an effect of alpha-1 stimulation in the eye, not a clonidine dry-mouth effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reflex tachycardia is not the described symptom and is not a listed clonidine effect.

questions.stem: In addition to treating hypertension, clonidine is used as an adjunct for which of the following conditions?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupil dilation for a dilated retinal exam

explanation.summary: Clonidine's reduction of central norepinephrine makes it useful as an ADHD adjunct.
explanation.whyCorrect: By decreasing norepinephrine release in the brain, clonidine can help control unwanted behaviors in psychiatric conditions such as ADHD and Tourette syndrome, and it is used as an adjunct treatment for ADHD.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Circulatory shock is treated with alpha-1 vasopressors like phenylephrine, not clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Facial erythema is treated with topical oxymetazoline, not clonidine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nasal congestion is treated with alpha-1 agonists such as phenylephrine or oxymetazoline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupil dilation is produced by alpha-1 agonists acting on the iris, not by clonidine.

questions.stem: Compared with norepinephrine and epinephrine, phenylephrine has a longer duration of action. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a selective alpha-2 agonist that resists enzymatic breakdown

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is highly protein bound in plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not a catecholamine and therefore is not metabolized by COMT

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is rapidly recycled by neuronal reuptake

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine escapes COMT metabolism because it is not a catecholamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike norepinephrine and epinephrine, phenylephrine is not a catecholamine, so it is not metabolized by catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). This gives it a longer duration of action.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its longer action is due to slower metabolism, not irreversible receptor binding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1, not alpha-2, agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the longer duration to lack of COMT metabolism, not protein binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Escape from COMT metabolism, not neuronal recycling, explains the longer effect.

questions.stem: During an infusion of intravenous phenylephrine, the drug leaks out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Which of the following complications is most likely?

explanation.summary: Extravasated phenylephrine causes intense local vasoconstriction and tissue necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peripheral extravasation of phenylephrine into surrounding tissue leads to excessive vasoconstriction, which can cause skin necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Its alpha-1 action raises pressure and constricts local vessels rather than causing local hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine constricts vessels; extravasation causes ischemia, not vasodilation and warmth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extravasation causes a local tissue injury; the systemic reflex from phenylephrine is bradycardia, not tachycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Xerostomia is a clonidine effect, not a consequence of phenylephrine extravasation.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist applies phenylephrine drops before a retinal examination. Which of the following effects makes the drug useful for this purpose?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Miosis from contraction of the sphincter pupillae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mydriasis from stimulation of the iris dilator muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced intraocular pressure by increasing aqueous outflow

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine dilates the pupil by stimulating alpha-1 receptors on the iris dilator muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the dilator muscle of the iris causes mydriasis, which is why phenylephrine is used as a diagnostic tool in ophthalmologic investigations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenylephrine is not a corneal anesthetic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes its ophthalmic use to pupil dilation and vasoconstriction, not tear production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine causes mydriasis (dilation), not miosis (constriction).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Its ophthalmic role is pupil dilation for exams, not lowering intraocular pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements correctly contrasts alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors are presynaptic, while alpha-2 receptors are postsynaptic on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors couple to Gq, while alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic and couple to Gi to reduce norepinephrine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-1 receptors decrease cytosolic calcium, while alpha-2 receptors increase it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors couple to Gs and raise cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alpha-2 receptors are widely distributed near the sympathetic terminal, while alpha-1 receptors regulate neurotransmitter release

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 receptors are postsynaptic Gq receptors; alpha-2 are presynaptic Gi receptors that curb norepinephrine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 receptors are widely distributed in the immediate vicinity of the sympathetic terminal and are Gq-coupled, whereas alpha-2 receptors are presynaptic, couple to Gi, and regulate (reduce) the release of neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the locations; alpha-2 receptors are the presynaptic subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 activation increases cytosolic calcium through the Gq/IP3 pathway, not decreases it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1 receptors are Gq-coupled and alpha-2 are Gi-coupled; neither raises cAMP through Gs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the roles; alpha-1 receptors are near the terminal and alpha-2 receptors regulate neurotransmitter release.

questions.stem: Clonidine activates a Gi-coupled receptor on presynaptic sympathetic nerve terminals. Which of the following intracellular changes most directly follows receptor activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of phospholipase C with increased IP3

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased adenylyl cyclase activity with decreased cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased adenylyl cyclase activity with increased cAMP

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum

explanation.summary: Alpha-2 receptors are Gi-coupled: activation decreases adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and PKA activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alpha-2 receptor is a Gi-type GPCR. Gi activation decreases adenylyl cyclase activation, which decreases cAMP formation and in turn decreases protein kinase A (PKA) activation. This is the signaling step that underlies clonidine's reduction of norepinephrine release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phospholipase C activation with increased IP3 is the Gq pathway used by alpha-1 receptors, not the Gi pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased adenylyl cyclase and cAMP is the Gs response; Gi does the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gi activation decreases, not increases, PKA activation because cAMP falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum follows IP3 generation in the Gq pathway, not Gi activation.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is comparing the signaling pathways of Gs, Gi, and Gq G protein-coupled receptors. Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Gq pathway from the other two?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gq activates membrane-bound phospholipase C rather than the cAMP-PKA pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gq is the only pathway that activates adenylyl cyclase to generate cAMP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gq is the only pathway that changes protein kinase A activation downstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gq is the only pathway that decreases cAMP formation through adenylyl cyclase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gq lowers cytosolic calcium while Gs and Gi both raise it through IP3

explanation.summary: Gi and Gs both signal through cAMP and PKA, whereas Gq signals through phospholipase C and cytosolic calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gi and Gs signal with the cAMP to protein kinase A pathway (Gs increasing and Gi decreasing it). Gq-type GPCRs instead activate membrane-bound phospholipase C, which raises IP3 and increases cytosolic calcium.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Activating adenylyl cyclase is the Gs pathway, not Gq.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both Gs and Gi change PKA activation (up and down, respectively); Gq does not work through PKA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreasing cAMP formation is the Gi pathway, not Gq.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gq increases cytosolic calcium; Gs and Gi act through cAMP rather than calcium.

questions.stem: Alpha-1 agonists such as phenylephrine are classified as sympathomimetics. Which of the following best describes why these drugs are primarily used clinically?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their ability to block muscarinic receptors in the airway

choices.label: B
