choices.text: Their ability to decrease norepinephrine release in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their action on cardiac beta-1 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their action on skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their action on the smooth muscle of the vasculature

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 agonists mimic sympathetic tone and are used mainly for their effect on vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sympathomimetics mimic the sympathetic tone. Alpha-1 agonists are primarily used due to their action on the smooth muscle vasculature, where alpha-1 stimulation causes vasoconstriction and raises blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are adrenergic agonists, not muscarinic antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreasing norepinephrine release in the brain is the alpha-2 agonist mechanism (clonidine, methyldopa).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 agonists like phenylephrine are selective for alpha-1 receptors, not cardiac beta-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1 agonists act on adrenergic receptors of vascular smooth muscle, not skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man in circulatory shock is treated with intravenous phenylephrine. As the infusion rate is increased, his arterial blood pressure rises further. Which of the following best characterizes the relationship between phenylephrine dose and blood pressure in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood pressure falls at higher doses because of reflex vasodilation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood pressure rises because higher doses increase cardiac contractility

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood pressure rises because higher doses recruit alpha-2 receptors in the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood pressure rises in a dose-dependent manner from increasing vasoconstriction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blood pressure rises only after a threshold dose that blocks beta-2 receptors

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine produces a dose-dependent increase in arterial blood pressure through alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 induced calcium release increases smooth muscle vasoconstriction. This increase in vasoconstriction causes a dose-dependent increase in arterial blood pressure, which is why IV phenylephrine is used to raise blood pressure rapidly in very hypotensive patients such as those in circulatory shock.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes a dose-dependent rise in pressure, not a fall from reflex vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenylephrine's pressor effect comes from vascular smooth muscle contraction, not increased contractility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-2 receptor activation in the brain lowers, not raises, blood pressure; phenylephrine's pressor effect is peripheral alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist and does not act through beta-2 blockade.

questions.stem: Norepinephrine and phenylephrine are both used as vasopressors in hypotensive patients. Which of the following statements correctly compares the two agents at the alpha-1 receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both drugs act as antagonists at the alpha-1 receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Norepinephrine has a higher affinity for the alpha-1 receptor than phenylephrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only norepinephrine acts as an agonist at the alpha-1 receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only phenylephrine acts as an agonist at the alpha-1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylephrine has a higher affinity for the alpha-1 receptor than norepinephrine

explanation.summary: Both are alpha-1 agonists, but phenylephrine binds the alpha-1 receptor with higher affinity than norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Norepinephrine and phenylephrine are both alpha-1 agonists that can potentially increase blood pressure in circulatory shock. Phenylephrine has a higher affinity for the receptor than norepinephrine. How and when each is used depends on factors such as heart rate, blood pressure, and renal function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both drugs are agonists, not antagonists, at alpha-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the relationship; phenylephrine is the higher-affinity agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenylephrine is also an alpha-1 agonist, and in fact a selective one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norepinephrine is also an alpha-1 agonist.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman uses over-the-counter oxymetazoline eye drops for minor eye irritation and redness. Which of the following best explains the relief she experiences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction of ocular vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-2 mediated reduction of norepinephrine release in the eye

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-2 mediated relaxation of the ciliary muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of histamine receptors on the conjunctiva

explanation.summary: Oxymetazoline is an alpha-1 agonist whose vasoconstriction relieves minor eye irritation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxymetazoline is another example of an alpha-1 agonist. It causes vasoconstriction by activating alpha-1 receptors, and its eye drops can be used to relieve minor eye irritation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxymetazoline is an alpha-1 agonist; reducing norepinephrine release is an alpha-2 mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Its effect is alpha-1 vasoconstriction, not beta-2 smooth muscle relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is not an antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes its ocular use to vasoconstriction, not aqueous humor production.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman seeks treatment for persistent facial erythema. Which of the following alpha-agonist formulations is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Topical oxymetazoline cream is used to treat facial erythema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxymetazoline causes vasoconstriction by activating alpha-1 receptors, and facial erythema can be treated using oxymetazoline topical cream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist used for hypertension and ADHD, not facial erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methyldopa is an alpha-2 agonist indicated for hypertension in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IV norepinephrine is a vasopressor for circulatory shock, not for facial erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IV phenylephrine is a vasopressor for hypotension, not a treatment for facial redness.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension has been using an intranasal alpha-1 agonist decongestant several times daily for a week. At a clinic visit his blood pressure is markedly elevated compared with baseline. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reflex bradycardia increased his stroke volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug blocked alpha-2 receptors on sympathetic terminals

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug caused sodium retention through renal beta-1 stimulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug constricted peripheral arterioles outside the nasal cavity

choices.label: E
choices.text: The drug increased norepinephrine release in the brainstem

explanation.summary: Decongestant alpha-1 agonists can cause hypertension when they constrict peripheral arterioles beyond the nose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 receptor agonists have side effects because they stimulate alpha-1 receptors outside of the nasal cavity. Constricting peripheral arterioles produces hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reflex bradycardia is a response to a rise in pressure, not the cause of the hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug is an alpha-1 agonist, not an alpha-2 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 agonists such as phenylephrine do not act through renal beta-1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-1 decongestants act directly on vascular alpha-1 receptors; they do not increase brainstem norepinephrine release.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman taking an oral phenylephrine-containing cold product reports feeling unusually anxious and jittery. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of the drug to alpha-1 receptors on neurons in the brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced norepinephrine release from presynaptic neurons in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reflex tachycardia from baroreceptor unloading as blood pressure falls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulation of alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem vasomotor center

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction of the nasal mucosa by local alpha-1 agonism

explanation.summary: Anxiety from alpha-1 decongestants results from the drug binding to neurons in the brain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 receptor agonists stimulate alpha-1 receptors outside the nasal cavity. When they bind to neurons in the brain, they can cause anxiety.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced norepinephrine release is the alpha-2 agonist effect, which produces sedation rather than anxiety.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the anxiety to central neuronal binding, not to a reflex heart-rate change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-2 stimulation in the brainstem lowers sympathetic outflow and would not produce anxiety.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nasal vasoconstriction is the intended decongestant effect, not the cause of anxiety.

questions.stem: A patient asks whether he should take an oral phenylephrine tablet or use a phenylephrine nasal spray for his congestion. Which of the following statements most accurately reflects the recent regulatory assessment of phenylephrine as a decongestant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both oral and intranasal phenylephrine were found ineffective at recommended doses and have been removed from the market

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intranasal phenylephrine lacks evidence of effectiveness at recommended doses, while the finding does not apply to oral use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral phenylephrine is effective at recommended doses only when combined with other active ingredients in combination products

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral phenylephrine lacks evidence of effectiveness at recommended doses, while the finding does not apply to intranasal use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenylephrine was found unsafe at recommended doses because of a risk of skin necrosis at the site of administration

explanation.summary: An FDA advisory committee found no scientific evidence that oral phenylephrine works as a nasal decongestant; the finding applies to oral, not intranasal, products.
explanation.whyCorrect: An FDA Advisory Committee determined that there is no scientific evidence supporting the effectiveness of oral phenylephrine as a nasal decongestant at the recommended dosages. These recommendations pertain only to orally administered phenylephrine, and the FDA will review the evidence before making any decision on its status.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The committee's finding concerned oral products only, and the FDA is still reviewing before deciding on the drug's status.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the finding; the concern is oral phenylephrine, not intranasal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The committee found no evidence of effectiveness for oral phenylephrine; the finding was not about combination products being more effective.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The issue was lack of effectiveness, not safety; skin necrosis relates to IV extravasation, not decongestant use.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Tourette syndrome has frequent motor and vocal tics. His physician prescribes a drug that reduces norepinephrine stimulation in the brain to help control these unwanted behaviors. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Clonidine's reduction of central norepinephrine stimulation is used for Tourette syndrome as well as ADHD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Other indications of clonidine include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and Tourette syndrome. Reducing norepinephrine stimulation in the brain may help control unwanted behaviors associated with these psychiatric conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Methyldopa is an alpha-2 agonist indicated only for hypertension during pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine is a vasopressor; increasing norepinephrine would not control these behaviors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-1 agonist for eye irritation and facial erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist vasopressor and decongestant with no role in Tourette syndrome.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man undergoing treatment for opioid use disorder with buprenorphine develops nausea, sweating, and anxiety during withdrawal. His physician adds an off-label adjunct medication to decrease these autonomic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely adjunct?

explanation.summary: Clonidine is used off-label as an adjunct to decrease the autonomic symptoms of opioid withdrawal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Off-label, clonidine is used in the treatment of opioid withdrawal as an adjunct with other agents such as methadone or buprenorphine. The use of clonidine decreases the autonomic symptoms of withdrawal, including nausea and anxiety.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-methylnorepinephrine is the active metabolite of methyldopa, not a drug given for withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methyldopa is an alpha-2 agonist whose only indication is hypertension during pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-1 agonist for eye irritation and facial erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist vasopressor; it has no role in opioid withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman started on clonidine for hypertension reports that she feels sleepy throughout the day. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of histamine H1 receptors in the brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of dopamine in the substantia nigra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased norepinephrine activity at central alpha-1 receptors

explanation.summary: Sedation is a major adverse effect of alpha-2 agonists, likely from reduced norepinephrine in the brain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sedation is a major adverse effect of alpha-2 agonists, likely resulting from reduced norepinephrine in the brain. Dizziness and fatigue can also occur with clonidine use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist, not an antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes sedation to reduced norepinephrine, not dopamine depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clonidine decreases, not increases, central norepinephrine activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clonidine's sedation is a central effect of lower norepinephrine, not a consequence of reflex bradycardia.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman is started on clonidine for hypertension. Two weeks later her family reports that she has become confused, lightheaded, and has fallen twice at home. Which of the following best describes this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An expected and self-limited side effect of alpha-2 agonists that requires no change in dose or management

choices.label: B
choices.text: The anxiety and agitation produced by alpha-1 stimulation of neurons in the brain, a common side effect in the elderly

choices.label: C
choices.text: The increased risk of mental status changes, dizziness, and falls that alpha-2 agonists carry in elderly individuals

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reflex tachycardia and palpitations that alpha-1 agonists typically produce in older patients with stiff vasculature

choices.label: E
choices.text: The skin necrosis that follows peripheral extravasation of the drug, which older patients with fragile veins are prone to

explanation.summary: In elderly individuals, alpha-2 agonists increase the risk of mental status changes, dizziness, and falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of alpha-2 agonists include xerostomia, sedation, and hypotension, and in elderly individuals there is an increased risk for mental status changes, dizziness, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Confusion and recurrent falls in an elderly patient are significant adverse effects, not a benign expected finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anxiety from central neuronal binding is an alpha-1 decongestant adverse effect, not a clonidine effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist, and it decreases rather than increases heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin necrosis from extravasation is a complication of IV phenylephrine, not oral clonidine.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with hypertension uncontrolled on lisinopril and amlodipine is being started on clonidine. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling point for this new medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expect a faster heart rate and more daytime energy within the first week

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expect increased salivation and drooling, which usually resolves within a week

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stay hydrated for dry mouth and expect occasional dizziness and fatigue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop taking amlodipine and lisinopril once clonidine is started

choices.label: E
choices.text: Watch for skin discoloration and ulceration at the site of each dose

explanation.summary: Clonidine counseling covers xerostomia (stay hydrated), occasional dizziness and fatigue, and a follow-up blood pressure check.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients started on clonidine should be counseled that the drug can cause dry mouth (xerostomia) and that they should stay hydrated, that they may get dizzy occasionally and feel tired, and that they should book a follow-up appointment to check blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine decreases sympathetic outflow and can decrease heart rate; sedation and fatigue, not more energy, are expected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonidine causes dryness of the mouth, not increased salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clonidine is being added to the existing regimen because blood pressure is uncontrolled; the other agents are not stopped.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin injury at an administration site relates to IV phenylephrine extravasation, not oral clonidine.

questions.stem: Both clonidine and intravenous phenylephrine can lower a patient's heart rate. Which of the following correctly contrasts the mechanism of the heart-rate decrease produced by each drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both drugs lower heart rate by directly stimulating alpha-1 receptors on pacemaker cells of the sinoatrial node, slowing phase 4 depolarization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both drugs lower heart rate by increasing systemic vascular resistance and loading the baroreceptors, which reduces sympathetic outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clonidine lowers heart rate by blocking cardiac beta-1 receptors; phenylephrine lowers it by decreasing systemic vascular resistance and unloading the baroreceptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clonidine lowers heart rate by decreasing sympathetic outflow centrally; phenylephrine lowers it through a baroreceptor reflex triggered by increased SVR

choices.label: E
choices.text: Clonidine lowers heart rate through a baroreceptor reflex triggered by increased SVR; phenylephrine lowers it by decreasing central sympathetic outflow

explanation.summary: Clonidine slows the heart by cutting central sympathetic outflow; phenylephrine slows it reflexively after raising SVR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clonidine activates presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, decreasing norepinephrine release and sympathetic outflow, and can decrease heart rate. Phenylephrine instead increases alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance, which causes a baroreceptor-mediated decrease in sympathetic outflow and reflex bradycardia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither drug slows the heart by direct alpha-1 action on the SA node; phenylephrine's effect is reflex and clonidine's is central.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonidine lowers rather than raises SVR; only phenylephrine acts through increased SVR and the baroreceptor reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clonidine is not a beta-blocker, and phenylephrine increases rather than decreases SVR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the two mechanisms.

questions.stem: Clonidine and methyldopa are both alpha-2 agonists used to lower blood pressure but work with slightly different mechanisms on the receptor. Which of the following best describes the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonidine acts on alpha-2 receptors in the brain, whereas methyldopa acts only on peripheral vascular alpha-2 receptors on smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clonidine acts on postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, whereas methyldopa acts on presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clonidine decreases norepinephrine release from nerve terminals, whereas methyldopa increases norepinephrine release from those same terminals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clonidine directly activates alpha-2 receptors, whereas methyldopa is metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine that is released as a false neurotransmitter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Clonidine must first be metabolized to an active metabolite that is released as a false neurotransmitter, whereas methyldopa directly activates alpha-2 receptors

explanation.summary: Clonidine is itself the alpha-2 agonist; methyldopa becomes one only after conversion to alpha-methylnorepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clonidine activates alpha-2 receptors on presynaptic sympathetic nerve terminals directly. Methyldopa is taken up into sympathetic nerve terminals and metabolized to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, a selective alpha-2 agonist that is loaded into presynaptic vesicles and released in place of norepinephrine, which is why it is called a false neurotransmitter.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Methyldopa's metabolite activates presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, not only peripheral vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both drugs act through presynaptic alpha-2 receptors; neither is an alpha-1 agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both drugs decrease sympathetic outflow and available norepinephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the drugs; methyldopa, not clonidine, requires metabolic conversion.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with essential hypertension asks whether methyldopa could be used to treat his blood pressure. Which of the following statements about methyldopa's clinical use is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because it constricts cutaneous vessels, it is used topically for the facial erythema of rosacea

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because it is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist, it is used as an adjunct for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because it lowers central sympathetic outflow, it is a first-line agent for essential hypertension in men

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because its onset is rapid and it is given intravenously, it is indicated only for hypertensive emergencies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Despite a mechanism that could treat any hypertension, it is indicated only for hypertension during pregnancy

explanation.summary: Methyldopa's mechanism would lower any blood pressure, but its only indication is hypertension during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: While its mechanism might indicate that methyldopa can be used in the treatment of all types of hypertension, it is only indicated and used in the treatment of hypertension during pregnancy, particularly for pregnant patients who develop adverse effects or become intolerant to other, more commonly used medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topical treatment of facial erythema is a use of oxymetazoline cream.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ADHD adjunct therapy is an indication of clonidine, not methyldopa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methyldopa is not a first-line agent for essential hypertension; its use is limited to pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe methyldopa as a hypertensive-emergency drug.

questions.stem: An alpha-1 agonist binds its receptor on a vascular smooth muscle cell and IP3 is generated. The calcium that then drives contraction is released from which of the following structures?

explanation.summary: IP3 releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum to trigger smooth muscle contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 receptor activation of phospholipase C converts PIP2 to IP3, and IP3 causes the release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting sustained increase in cytosolic calcium produces smooth muscle contraction and vasoconstriction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The Golgi apparatus is not the IP3-responsive calcium store in this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysosomes are not the source of the calcium released by IP3.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick identifies the endoplasmic reticulum, not mitochondria, as the IP3-sensitive calcium store.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The nucleus is not the source of calcium in the alpha-1 signaling pathway.

questions.stem: Phenylephrine eye drops are applied and the conjunctival redness in a patient's eye noticeably decreases. Which of the following structures is directly responsible for this specific change?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radial dilator muscle of the iris

choices.label: E
choices.text: Circular sphincter muscle of the iris

explanation.summary: Phenylephrine reduces eye redness by constricting alpha-1 bearing conjunctival arterioles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylephrine stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors within the eye. Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the dilator muscle causes mydriasis, while stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the arterioles of the conjunctiva causes vasoconstriction, which reduces conjunctival redness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The ciliary muscle is not an alpha-1 target described for phenylephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The corneal epithelium is not involved in the vascular response to phenylephrine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-1 stimulation of the dilator muscle produces mydriasis, not decreased redness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine does not act on the sphincter muscle, which mediates miosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in the emergency department has a blood pressure of 68/40 mm Hg due to circulatory shock. Which of the following agents is most appropriate to rapidly increase his blood pressure?

explanation.summary: IV phenylephrine is used in acute care to rapidly raise blood pressure in circulatory shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylephrine's alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction produces a dose-dependent increase in arterial blood pressure. This is useful in acute care scenarios for patients who are very hypotensive, usually in circulatory shock, where IV phenylephrine is used to increase blood pressure rapidly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intranasal phenylephrine is a decongestant; the vasopressor use is intravenous.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist that lowers blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyldopa lowers blood pressure and is indicated only for hypertension in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical oxymetazoline is used for eye irritation and facial erythema, not systemic hypotension.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to predict the adverse effect profiles of an alpha-1 agonist vasopressor and a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist. Which of the following pairs correctly matches each class with an adverse effect characteristic of it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-1 agonist: hypotension; alpha-2 agonist: hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-1 agonist: mental status changes in the elderly; alpha-2 agonist: anxiety

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alpha-1 agonist: reflex bradycardia; alpha-2 agonist: sedation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alpha-1 agonist: sedation; alpha-2 agonist: skin necrosis with extravasation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alpha-1 agonist: xerostomia; alpha-2 agonist: reflex bradycardia

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 vasopressors cause reflex bradycardia and extravasation injury; alpha-2 agonists cause sedation, xerostomia, and hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of alpha-1 receptor agonists such as phenylephrine include reflex bradycardia and extravasation. Adverse effects of alpha-2 agonists include xerostomia, sedation, hypotension, and in elderly individuals an increased risk of mental status changes, dizziness, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is reversed; alpha-1 agonists raise blood pressure and alpha-2 agonists can cause hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mental status changes in the elderly are an alpha-2 agonist risk, and anxiety is an alpha-1 decongestant effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This swaps the effects: sedation belongs to alpha-2 agonists and extravasation necrosis to IV alpha-1 agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This swaps the effects: xerostomia is an alpha-2 effect and reflex bradycardia an alpha-1 effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the signaling cascade that follows activation of a Gs-coupled G protein-coupled receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated adenylyl cyclase, increased cAMP, increased PKA activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activated guanylyl cyclase, increased cGMP, smooth muscle relaxation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activated phospholipase C, decreased cAMP, decreased cytosolic calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activated phospholipase C, increased IP3, increased cytosolic calcium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased adenylyl cyclase, decreased cAMP, decreased PKA activation

explanation.summary: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and PKA activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gs-type receptors activate adenylyl cyclase, which increases cAMP and in turn increases protein kinase A (PKA) activation. Gi does the opposite along the same cAMP-PKA pathway, and Gq works through phospholipase C instead.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Guanylyl cyclase and cGMP are not part of the Gs pathway described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phospholipase C is a Gq effector, and Gs raises rather than lowers cAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipase C, IP3, and calcium is the Gq cascade (alpha-1 receptors).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and PKA is the Gi cascade (alpha-2 receptors).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man was recently started on a new antihypertensive. He now reports dry mouth, daytime sleepiness, and lightheadedness, and his blood pressure is lower than his target. Which of the following drugs was most likely added?

explanation.summary: Xerostomia, sedation, and hypotension together point to an alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine include xerostomia, sedation, hypotension, dizziness, and fatigue. Sedation likely results from reduced norepinephrine in the brain, and the fall in sympathetic outflow can lower blood pressure excessively.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, not the alpha-2 agonist that produces this profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor and is not the drug the brick associates with xerostomia and sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxymetazoline is a topical alpha-1 agonist for eye irritation and facial erythema, not an antihypertensive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that raises blood pressure and would not be used as an antihypertensive.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is started on an α1-adrenergic blocker to relieve his urinary hesitancy and weak stream. The therapeutic effect of this drug class is achieved primarily by blocking α1-receptors on which of the following structures?

explanation.summary: α1-Blockade relieves BPH symptoms by relaxing prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Receptors are densely expressed in prostatic smooth muscle, and the α1A subtype in particular is abundant in the prostate and urinary tract. Blocking these receptors relaxes the smooth muscle, dilates the urethra, and decreases resistance to urine flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal gland has no notable α1-receptors relevant to this drug's action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although α-receptors exist in the cerebral cortex, blockade there is not clinically relevant to BPH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: α1-Blockade does not act on the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle is not a target of α1-adrenergic blockers.

questions.stem: A urologist wants to prescribe an α1-blocker whose selectivity for the α1A subtype makes it especially suited to treating benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following agents is the α1A-selective (uroselective) blocker?

explanation.summary: Tamsulosin is the α1A-selective, uroselective blocker used for BPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because α1A-receptor expression in the prostate and urinary tract is high, tamsulosin—an α1A blocker—is often prescribed for BPH. Its uroselectivity gives it strong effects on the lower urinary tract with relatively little effect on vascular tone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker used for hypertension and BPH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective α (α1 and α2) antagonist used for pheochromocytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker used mainly for hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker, not α1A-selective.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and a history of falls needs an α1-blocker that carries the lowest risk of orthostatic hypotension. Which of the following agents is the best choice?

explanation.summary: Tamsulosin has the lowest risk of orthostatic hypotension because of its α1A selectivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tamsulosin's selective affinity for α1A receptors in the lower urinary tract spares vascular α1-receptors, so it has the lowest risk of orthostatic hypotension. This makes it favorable in older patients prone to falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker that decreases peripheral resistance and can cause orthostatic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective α-antagonist that markedly lowers blood pressure and is not used for BPH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prazosin has high affinity for α1-receptors and rapid onset, giving it the highest first-dose orthostatic hypotension risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker that lowers blood pressure and can cause orthostatic hypotension.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with episodic headaches, palpitations, and severe hypertension is diagnosed with pheochromocytoma and started on phenoxybenzamine before surgical resection. This drug is effective in pheochromocytoma because it acts as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective (α1 and α2) antagonist used before pheochromocytoma surgery.
explanation.whyCorrect: By blocking both α1 and α2 receptors, phenoxybenzamine decreases total peripheral resistance and blood pressure, countering the catecholamine surge from the tumor. Its irreversible binding gives longer, more pronounced effects than reversible agents.

whyWrongByChoice.B: It is not limited to α1; it also blocks α2, which is central to its use here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is not α1-selective; nonselective α-blockade is what controls the catecholamine surge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective α2-blockade would not effectively lower the catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is not a β-blocker; β-blockade must not be given first in pheochromocytoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is started on prazosin for hypertension. Shortly after his first dose he stands up and becomes lightheaded and nearly faints. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bladder smooth muscle relaxation reduces venous return

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iris dilator muscle atrophy reduces cerebral perfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: α2-Agonism reduces norepinephrine release in the CNS, causing sedation

choices.label: E
choices.text: β1-Blockade slows the heart rate excessively

explanation.summary: Prazosin's first-dose orthostatic hypotension results from α1-mediated vasodilation with an inadequate baroreflex response.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Blockers inhibit vascular smooth muscle contraction, causing vasodilation. The compensatory baroreflex fails to sufficiently increase sympathetic outflow, so blood pressure drops on standing, producing syncope and dizziness. Prazosin's high α1 affinity and rapid onset make this most pronounced with the first dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bladder relaxation causes ejaculatory problems, not a drop in venous return or blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iris dilator atrophy causes floppy iris syndrome, not orthostatic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α2-Agonism describes centrally acting drugs like clonidine, not the mechanism of prazosin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prazosin is an α1-blocker and does not block β1-receptors or slow the heart.

questions.stem: A patient with pheochromocytoma is being prepared for surgery. A trainee suggests starting a β-blocker first to control the tachycardia. The attending warns this order is dangerous. Which of the following best explains why α-blockade must precede β-blockade?

choices.label: A
choices.text: α-Blockade first increases catecholamine release from the tumor, which β-blockade then suppresses

choices.label: B
choices.text: α-Blockers become ineffective at vascular receptors once β-receptors have been blocked

choices.label: C
choices.text: β-Blockade first causes reflex bradycardia that stops the tumor from secreting catecholamines into the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: β-Blockade first irreversibly blocks α2-receptors on presynaptic sympathetic nerve terminals

choices.label: E
choices.text: β-Blockade first removes β-mediated vasodilation, leaving unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction

explanation.summary: In pheochromocytoma, α-blockade must come before β-blockade to avoid unopposed α vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Giving a β-blocker first knocks out the vasodilatory effect of β-adrenergic receptors while circulating catecholamines still stimulate α1-receptors. The result is unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis, so α-blockade is initiated first, followed by β-blockade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: α-Blockade does not increase catecholamine release in the way described; the danger is unopposed vasoconstriction from β-first dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: α-Blockers remain effective; the issue is the hemodynamic consequence of β-blockade given first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: β-Blockade does not stop the tumor from secreting catecholamines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: β-Blockers do not irreversibly block α2-receptors; this is not the concern.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man undergoing cataract surgery develops a billowing, poorly dilating iris that prolapses during the procedure (intraoperative floppy iris syndrome). This complication is most strongly associated with chronic use of which of the following drugs?

explanation.summary: Tamsulosin carries the highest risk of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: IFIS is caused by inhibition of iris dilator smooth muscle contraction and atrophy from α1-receptor blockade, most often seen in cataract surgery. Tamsulosin is particularly associated with IFIS and carries the highest risk of any α1-blocker.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker with lower IFIS risk than tamsulosin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenoxybenzamine is used for pheochromocytoma and is not the classic IFIS culprit.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phentolamine is a nonselective α-antagonist used for pheochromocytoma, not linked to IFIS in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prazosin can cause floppy iris but is far less associated with it than tamsulosin.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man taking tamsulosin for BPH reports that during orgasm he produces little or no semen, and his urine afterward appears cloudy. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased sympathetic tone closes the internal urethral sphincter during emission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolonged smooth muscle contraction traps semen within the prostatic ducts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxation of bladder smooth muscle allows semen to be propelled backward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vasodilation of the penile arteries prevents erection and forward emission

choices.label: E
choices.text: α2-Receptor stimulation blocks the emission phase of semen from the vas deferens

explanation.summary: α1-Blockers like tamsulosin can cause retrograde ejaculation by relaxing bladder smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some α1-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin, silodosin) relax the bladder and impair the smooth-muscle contraction that propels semen forward. Without forward propulsion, semen is directed backward into the bladder—retrograde ejaculation—explaining the cloudy post-orgasm urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: α1-Blockade relaxes, not tightens, the internal sphincter; increased sympathetic tone is not the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug relaxes rather than contracts smooth muscle, so semen is not trapped by contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes an erectile effect, not the retrograde ejaculation the patient is experiencing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The effect is due to α1-blockade relaxing bladder smooth muscle, not α2-receptor stimulation.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man taking tamsulosin for BPH asks his physician about starting sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. The physician cautions that combining these drugs can be dangerous. Which of the following adverse outcomes is of greatest concern?

explanation.summary: Combining an α1-blocker with a PDE-5 inhibitor risks severe additive hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Blockers with other vasodilatory agents can cause significant hypotension. Concomitant use with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil can precipitate severe hypotension, which may lead to loss of consciousness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: α1-Blockers relieve urinary retention in BPH rather than cause it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The combined vasodilatory effect lowers, not raises, blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Priapism is a rare α1-blocker effect but is not the drug-interaction concern with sildenafil described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The primary danger is hypotension from additive vasodilation, not a tachyarrhythmia.

questions.stem: A man with benign prostatic hyperplasia reports urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and incomplete voiding. His physician explains that α1-blockers improve these symptoms. Which of the following best describes how these drugs relieve his obstruction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They contract the detrusor muscle to forcefully expel urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: They increase urine production by acting on the kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: They relax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: They shrink the prostate gland by blocking androgen receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: They tighten the urethral sphincter to improve continence

explanation.summary: α1-Blockers treat BPH obstruction by relaxing prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In BPH, α1-receptor activation in prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle causes contraction that obstructs the urethra. Blocking these receptors relaxes the smooth muscle, dilates the urethra, and decreases the resistance to urine flow, improving the urinary symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They relax smooth muscle rather than contract the detrusor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: They act on lower urinary tract smooth muscle, not on renal urine production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not block androgen receptors or shrink the gland; that describes 5α-reductase inhibitors or antiandrogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They relax rather than tighten the sphincter, reducing outflow resistance.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student reviews how α1-receptor blockade produces vasodilation. α1-Receptors are coupled to which of the following G proteins, whose downstream signaling is blocked by these drugs?

explanation.summary: α1-Receptors are Gq-coupled, signaling through Ca2+ and calmodulin-sensitive pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Receptors belong to the Gq type of GPCR, and most of their actions are mediated by Ca2+ and calmodulin (CaM)-sensitive pathways that drive smooth-muscle contraction. Blocking α1 reduces this Ca2+/CaM-driven actin-myosin interaction, causing vasodilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gi is coupled to α2-receptors, which inhibit adenylyl cyclase, not α1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Golf is an olfactory G protein, unrelated to α1-adrenergic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gs is coupled to receptors such as β-adrenergic receptors, not α1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gt (transducin) mediates phototransduction in the retina, not α1 signaling.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has both stage 1 hypertension and mild benign prostatic hyperplasia. His physician wants a single nonselective α1-blocker that is approved to treat both conditions. Which of the following agents best fits?

explanation.summary: Doxazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker approved for both hypertension and BPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-uroselective α1-blockers such as prazosin, terazosin, and doxazosin are used as antihypertensive agents. Doxazosin (along with terazosin) has additionally been approved for the treatment of BPH, making it suitable for a patient with both conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Phenoxybenzamine is a nonselective α-antagonist reserved for pheochromocytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phentolamine is a nonselective α-antagonist used for short-term BP control in pheochromocytoma, not chronic hypertension plus BPH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silodosin is a uroselective agent for BPH, not an antihypertensive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tamsulosin is an α1A-selective uroselective agent for BPH; it is not used as an antihypertensive.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is reviewing the tissue distribution of α1-adrenergic receptors. Sympathetic stimulation of α1-receptors causes contraction of which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronchiolar smooth muscle of the airways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciliary muscle of the eye controlling lens shape

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilator pupillae (radial) muscle of the eye

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sinoatrial nodal pacemaker tissue of the heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sphincter pupillae (circular) muscle of the eye

explanation.summary: α1-Receptors are found in the dilator pupillae (radial) muscle of the eye, along with arteriolar smooth muscle, GI and urinary sphincters, the urethra, and the prostate.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Receptors are expressed in the smooth muscle of arterioles, the gastrointestinal and urinary sphincters, the urethra, the prostate gland, and the dilator pupillae (radial) muscle of the eye. Because these receptors drive smooth-muscle contraction through Gq/Ca2+ signaling, α1 stimulation contracts the dilator pupillae, and α1-blockade impairs its contraction (the basis of floppy iris syndrome).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchiolar smooth muscle is not among the α1-receptor locations described for this drug class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ciliary muscle is not listed among the α1-receptor sites; it is not the α1-mediated contractile target in the eye.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sinoatrial nodal tissue is not an α1-receptor site; α1-blockers act on smooth muscle, not nodal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sphincter pupillae is not an α1 site; the α1-bearing iris muscle is the dilator (radial) muscle.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with hypertension is started on doxazosin and her blood pressure falls. In vascular smooth muscle, the drug's effect on blood pressure is ultimately produced by a decrease in which of the following intracellular events?

explanation.summary: α1-Blockade reduces cytosolic Ca2+ and calmodulin activation, decreasing actin-myosin binding and relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Receptor signaling raises cytosolic Ca2+, which increases calmodulin (CaM) activation and subsequently increases actin-myosin binding, producing smooth-muscle contraction of the vasculature. Inhibiting this Ca2+/CaM-sensitive pathway reverses the contraction and causes vasodilation, lowering peripheral vascular resistance and blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gi-mediated adenylyl cyclase inhibition describes α2-receptor signaling, not α1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: α1-Receptors signal through Gq and Ca2+/CaM, not through cAMP and protein kinase A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not act through the nitric oxide/cGMP pathway; that is the pathway relevant to PDE-5 inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The α1 pathway described is Ca2+/CaM-mediated contraction, not potassium channel hyperpolarization.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is prescribed alfuzosin. A student asks how this drug is classified. Which of the following correctly describes alfuzosin's classification by receptor selectivity and by clinical use, respectively?

explanation.summary: Alfuzosin is a nonselective α1-blocker by receptor selectivity but is grouped with tamsulosin as uroselective by clinical use.
explanation.whyCorrect: By receptor selectivity, the nonselective α1-blockers are prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin, and alfuzosin; only tamsulosin is the α1A-selective agent. By clinical use, the uroselective α1-blockers are tamsulosin and alfuzosin, while prazosin, terazosin, and doxazosin are non-uroselective. Alfuzosin therefore straddles the two schemes: nonselective among α1 subtypes, yet used uroselectively for BPH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nonselective α-blockers (α1 and α2) used in pheochromocytoma are phenoxybenzamine and phentolamine, not alfuzosin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alfuzosin is not a non-uroselective antihypertensive; the non-uroselective agents are prazosin, terazosin, and doxazosin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alfuzosin is an α1-blocker, not a selective α2-blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tamsulosin is the α1A-selective blocker; alfuzosin is not α1A-selective even though it is uroselective.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with a known pheochromocytoma awaiting surgery presents with a blood pressure of 230/130 mm Hg, flushing, and tachycardia. The team wants a reversible α-antagonist to provide short-term control of his hypertension. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Phentolamine is the reversible nonselective α-antagonist used for short-term control of hypertension in pheochromocytoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenoxybenzamine and phentolamine are the most common agents used for the initial management of pheochromocytoma before surgical resection; both are nonselective antagonists of α1- and α2-receptors. They differ in that phentolamine is reversible and is used for short-term control of hypertension in pheochromocytoma patients, whereas phenoxybenzamine binds irreversibly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible antagonist with much longer and more pronounced effects; it is used for long-term control rather than short-term control.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker used for hypertension, not the nonselective α-antagonist used in pheochromocytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tamsulosin is an α1A-selective uroselective agent for BPH with little effect on vascular tone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terazosin is a non-uroselective α1-blocker for hypertension and BPH, not a pheochromocytoma agent.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla is deemed inoperable because of severe comorbidities. Her physician wants an agent for long-term control of her blood pressure. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

explanation.summary: Phenoxybenzamine is used for long-term control in pheochromocytoma patients who are inoperable.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible nonselective α-antagonist, resulting in much longer and more pronounced effects than the reversible agent phentolamine. By blocking both α1- and α2-receptors it decreases total peripheral resistance and blood pressure, and it is specifically used for long-term control in patients with pheochromocytoma who are inoperable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker used for hypertension and BPH; nonselective α-blockers are the agents used in pheochromocytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phentolamine is reversible and used for short-term control of hypertension in pheochromocytoma, not long-term management.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silodosin is a uroselective α1-blocker used for BPH, not for catecholamine-secreting tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tamsulosin is an α1A-selective uroselective agent for BPH and is not used for pheochromocytoma.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has episodes of flushing, tachycardia, and severe hypertension. Laboratory studies confirm a very rare neuroendocrine, catecholamine-producing tumor. This tumor is usually found in which of the following locations?

explanation.summary: Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine-producing neuroendocrine tumor usually found in the adrenal medulla.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pheochromocytoma is a very rare neuroendocrine, catecholamine-producing tumor usually found in the adrenal medulla. A flood of endogenous catecholamines acting on α-receptors can result in a hypertensive crisis associated with flushing and tachycardia, although many patients just have high blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones, not the catecholamine flood of pheochromocytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The anterior pituitary is not the site of this catecholamine-producing tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic islets are endocrine tissue but are not the usual site of a catecholamine-producing tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thyroid gland does not produce catecholamines; pheochromocytoma arises in the adrenal medulla.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with newly diagnosed hypertension and no prostate symptoms asks whether he should be started on prazosin, a drug his neighbor takes. His physician explains that α1-blockers are generally not chosen as initial therapy for hypertension. Which of the following best explains this recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They act only on prostatic and not on vascular α1-receptors in the periphery

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cause reflex hypertension by blocking central α2-receptors in the brainstem

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have an unfavorable safety profile compared with other antihypertensives

choices.label: D
choices.text: They lose efficacy because vascular α1-receptors are rapidly upregulated during therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: They raise peripheral vascular resistance over the first months of therapy

explanation.summary: α1-Blockers can lower blood pressure but are not first-line antihypertensives because of their unfavorable safety profile.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Blockers may be used to lower blood pressure in patients with hypertension, but they are not first-line agents because of their unfavorable safety profile compared with other antihypertensive agents. Non-uroselective α1-blockers such as prazosin, doxazosin, and terazosin are used as antihypertensives, again not as first line.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-uroselective α1-blockers act on vascular α1-receptors, which is why they lower blood pressure at all.
whyWrongByChoice.B: α1-Blockers do not block central α2-receptors, and they lower rather than raise blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor upregulation causing loss of efficacy is not the reason the class is avoided as first line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: α1-Blockers decrease, not raise, peripheral vascular resistance; that is how they lower blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with resistant hypertension has doxazosin added to her regimen. Which of the following hemodynamic changes is directly responsible for the drug's antihypertensive effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased cardiac contractility through L-type Ca2+ channel blockade in myocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased heart rate through β1-receptor blockade at the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased peripheral vascular resistance through postsynaptic α1-receptor inhibition

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased plasma volume through inhibition of renal sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Decreased renin release through juxtaglomerular β1-receptor blockade in the kidney

explanation.summary: α1-Blockers lower blood pressure by inhibiting postsynaptic α1-receptors, which decreases peripheral vascular resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: α1-Receptor blockers such as doxazosin inhibit the activation of postsynaptic α1-receptors on vascular smooth muscle. By inhibiting α1-receptor function, peripheral vascular resistance is decreased, and thus blood pressure decreases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The drug does not block Ca2+ channels or reduce contractility; it reduces resistance in the vasculature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxazosin is an α1-blocker; it does not block β1-receptors or slow the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not act as diuretics or reduce plasma volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renin suppression through β1-blockade is a β-blocker mechanism, not an α1-blocker mechanism.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man took terazosin for 2 years for benign prostatic hyperplasia without dizziness. He stopped the drug for 3 weeks while traveling, then resumed it at his previous full dose. That evening he fainted on standing. Which of the following best explains this event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of terazosin from impaired hepatic clearance over the three-week break

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of terazosin to an α2-agonist metabolite that lowers sympathetic nerve outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Development of tolerance to terazosin's urinary effects over two years of use

choices.label: D
choices.text: Re-dosing after discontinuation restores the first-dose orthostatic hypotension risk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withdrawal-induced rebound hypertension from the three-week treatment interruption

explanation.summary: Re-dosing an α1-blocker after discontinuation is a recognized risk factor for orthostatic hypotension, like a first dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Risk factors for orthostatic hypotension with α1-blockers include the first dose or re-dose after discontinuation, a rapid increase in dose, concurrent medications that cause OH (nitrates, PDE-5 inhibitors), and the type of α1-blocker. Restarting terazosin at the full prior dose after a 3-week break re-creates the first-dose situation, in which vasodilation is not compensated by a baroreflex increase in sympathetic outflow, causing syncope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no indication of impaired clearance; the timing after re-dosing points to the first-dose phenomenon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Terazosin is not converted to an α2-agonist; the mechanism is α1-blockade-induced vasodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance to urinary effects would not cause syncope; the event is orthostatic hypotension from re-dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient fainted from hypotension, not rebound hypertension.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man is being discharged on a new prescription for doxazosin. Which of the following instructions is most important to reduce his risk of falls related to this medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoid all dairy products within 2 hours of dosing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rise slowly from sitting or lying positions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stop the drug immediately if urine appears cloudy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Take the medication with a high-fat meal

explanation.summary: Patients on α1-blockers should be instructed to rise slowly from sitting or supine positions to reduce orthostatic hypotension and falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Orthostatic hypotension is one of the main adverse effects of this drug class and can lead to an increased risk of falls, especially in frail older adults. Patients should be instructed to rise slowly from sitting or supine positions for as long as they are on these medications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dairy avoidance is unrelated to α1-blocker adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluid restriction does not address orthostatic hypotension and is not part of α1-blocker counseling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cloudy urine after orgasm reflects retrograde ejaculation, an ejaculatory effect, not a reason for abrupt discontinuation to prevent falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Taking the drug with a high-fat meal is not the fall-prevention counseling for α1-blockers.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia is prescribed tamsulosin. He has read that this drug is 'uroselective' and asks whether that means he cannot become lightheaded on standing. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tamsulosin carries no risk of lightheadedness because it acts only on receptors in the prostate and bladder neck

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tamsulosin carries no risk of lightheadedness because it is an α2-selective agent rather than an α1-blocker

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tamsulosin has the highest risk of orthostatic hypotension among α1-blockers because of its rapid onset

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tamsulosin has the lowest risk among α1-blockers, but all α1-blockers carry a risk of orthostatic hypotension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tamsulosin has the same risk as prazosin because both are nonselective α1-blockers with equal receptor affinity

explanation.summary: All α1-blockers, uroselective or not, carry a risk of orthostatic hypotension; tamsulosin's α1A selectivity makes its risk the lowest, not zero.
explanation.whyCorrect: All α1-blockers (uro- or non-uroselective) carry the risk of orthostatic hypotension. Tamsulosin has the lowest risk because of its selective affinity for α1A receptors, which are highly expressed in the prostate and urinary tract, but the risk is reduced rather than eliminated, so counseling to rise slowly still applies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uroselectivity lowers but does not abolish the risk; the source states all α1-blockers carry OH risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tamsulosin is an α1A-selective blocker, not an α2-selective agent, and it still carries OH risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prazosin, with its high α1 affinity and rapid onset, has the higher risk; tamsulosin has the lowest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tamsulosin is α1A-selective, not nonselective, and its OH risk is lower than that of prazosin.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with stable angina and benign prostatic hyperplasia takes terazosin. His cardiologist adds a long-acting nitrate. Two days later he experiences dizziness and near-syncope when standing. Which of the following best explains this new symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Additive orthostatic hypotension from a concurrent vasodilatory medication

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coronary steal producing transient ischemic hypotension during standing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrate inhibition of terazosin's hepatic metabolism raising its drug levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nitrate-induced increase in α1-receptor affinity for terazosin in vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reflex bradycardia from combined baroreceptor stimulation by both drugs

explanation.summary: Concurrent medications that cause orthostatic hypotension, such as nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors, increase the OH risk of α1-blockers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the stated risk factors for orthostatic hypotension with α1-blockers are concurrent medications that can cause OH, specifically nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors. The combination of α1-receptor blockers with other vasodilatory agents may cause significant hypotension, so adding a nitrate to terazosin produces additive vasodilation and orthostatic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coronary steal is not the mechanism described for α1-blocker and nitrate co-administration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interaction is not a metabolic one; it results from two vasodilatory mechanisms acting together.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrates do not alter terazosin's receptor affinity; the interaction is pharmacodynamic (additive vasodilation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: The baroreflex fails to compensate adequately during α1-blockade; the problem is hypotension, not reflex bradycardia.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man taking an α1-blocker for benign prostatic hyperplasia is scheduled for cataract surgery. The ophthalmologist anticipates intraoperative floppy iris syndrome. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corneal endothelial dysfunction from reduced tear production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of iris dilator smooth muscle contraction with atrophy of the muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paralysis of the ciliary muscle with loss of accommodation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained contraction of the sphincter pupillae from unopposed cholinergic tone

explanation.summary: IFIS results from α1-blockade inhibiting iris dilator smooth muscle contraction and causing its atrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome is caused by the inhibition of iris dilator smooth muscle contraction due to α1-receptor inhibition, along with atrophy of that muscle. It is most often seen in patients undergoing cataract surgery, and tamsulosin carries the highest risk, though other α1-blockers are also implicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corneal and tear-film dysfunction are unrelated to α1-blockade of the iris dilator.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IFIS is a structural iris problem during surgery, not an intraocular pressure disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ciliary muscle and accommodation are not the α1-mediated targets involved in IFIS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IFIS is a failure of the dilator muscle, not a cholinergic overactivation of the sphincter pupillae.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a painful erection lasting 5 hours that began without sexual stimulation. He recently started a new medication for hypertension. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Priapism and prolonged erections are reported adverse effects associated with non-selective α1-blockers such as prazosin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the other adverse effects of α1-blockers, priapism and prolonged erections have been reported and are associated with the non-selective α1-blockers. Prazosin is a nonselective α1-blocker used as an antihypertensive, fitting a patient who recently started a blood pressure medication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonidine-type α2-agonists treat hypertension but their main adverse effect is sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Propranolol is a β-blocker and is not the α1-blocker class associated with priapism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silodosin is a uroselective BPH agent associated with ejaculation difficulties, not the antihypertensive linked to priapism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tamsulosin is the α1A-selective uroselective agent for BPH, not an antihypertensive, and its characteristic ejaculatory effect is retrograde ejaculation rather than priapism.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man taking tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia reports new erectile dysfunction and asks whether stopping tamsulosin would restore his erections. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stopping it is unlikely to help, because erections are primarily mediated by the parasympathetic system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stopping it will help, because retrograde ejaculation of semen into the bladder prevents erection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stopping it will help, because α1-blockade directly prevents penile arterial inflow during arousal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stopping it will help, because α1-blockade suppresses testosterone production by the testes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stopping it will not help, because tamsulosin does not reach the penile erectile tissue in the first place

explanation.summary: Tamsulosin is a sympatholytic drug; because erections are primarily parasympathetic, it does not generally affect erections and stopping it is unlikely to help.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although tamsulosin sometimes causes sexual side effects such as retrograde ejaculation, it does not generally affect erections, because it is a sympathetic (sympatholytic) drug and erections are primarily mediated by the parasympathetic system. Therefore stopping tamsulosin is not likely to improve his erectile dysfunction, which is more likely related to age or comorbid conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Retrograde ejaculation is an ejaculatory effect that does not prevent erection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: α1-Blockade causes vasodilation, not reduced arterial inflow, and does not generally impair erections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not suppress testosterone production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reason is not lack of tissue penetration; it is that erection is parasympathetically mediated and tamsulosin is a sympatholytic drug.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man started on terazosin 1 week ago for hypertension reports drowsiness, generalized weakness, and headache. He has had no syncope. Which of the following best explains his symptoms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Common adverse effects of α1-blocker therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serotonin syndrome from excess CNS serotonin

explanation.summary: Common adverse effects of α1-blockers include dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, drowsiness, weakness, and headache.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to orthostatic hypotension, the common adverse effects of α1-blockers are dizziness, drowsiness, weakness, and headache; they can also cause ejaculation difficulties. A cluster of drowsiness, weakness, and headache shortly after starting terazosin is therefore an expected adverse-effect profile of the drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Terazosin blocks α1-receptors, not muscarinic receptors; anticholinergic toxicity is not expected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unopposed α-stimulation and hypertensive crisis occur when β-blockade precedes α-blockade in pheochromocytoma, not with terazosin monotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not impair glycogenolysis or cause hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terazosin does not affect serotonin; serotonin syndrome is not an α1-blocker effect.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is prescribed a centrally acting α2-agonist. His parents ask about the most likely adverse effect. Which of the following is the main adverse effect of this drug class?

explanation.summary: α2-Agonists block norepinephrine release in the CNS; their main adverse effect is sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: α2-Agonists block norepinephrine release in the CNS and can be used to treat hypertension, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and substance withdrawal. Their main adverse effect is sedation, which distinguishes them from the α1-blockers whose main adverse effect is orthostatic hypotension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Floppy iris syndrome is caused by α1-blockade of the iris dilator, not by α2-agonism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Orthostatic hypotension from α1-blockade is the main adverse effect of α1-blockers, not of α2-agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Priapism is associated with non-selective α1-blockers, not α2-agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retrograde ejaculation is an adverse effect of α1-blockers such as tamsulosin and silodosin.

questions.stem: A pharmacology lecture describes drugs that antagonize α1-adrenergic receptors. Because they oppose the effects of norepinephrine at these receptors, α1-antagonists are classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: α1-Antagonists (α1-blockers) are sympatholytic drugs that affect α1-receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sympatholytic drugs that affect α1-receptors are called α1-antagonists or α1-blockers. They elicit their actions by inhibiting the function of α1-receptors, reducing the sympathetic (norepinephrine-mediated) contraction of smooth muscle in arterioles, sphincters, the urethra, and the prostate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: α1-Blockers act at postsynaptic α1-receptors, not at autonomic ganglia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parasympatholytics block muscarinic cholinergic transmission, not α1-adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasympathomimetics mimic acetylcholine; α1-blockers act on the sympathetic α1-receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sympathomimetics activate adrenergic receptors; α1-blockers inhibit them.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with an enlarged prostate has a compressed prostatic urethra and a tight bladder neck on imaging. The endogenous ligand whose action at α1-receptors maintains this bladder-neck and urethral smooth muscle contraction is which of the following?

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine activates α1-receptors on prostatic, urethral, and bladder-neck smooth muscle, causing contraction and urethral compression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Activation of α1-receptors in prostatic smooth muscle, the prostatic urethra, and the bladder neck by norepinephrine causes urethral and sphincter smooth muscle contraction, which decreases urine flow through the prostatic portion of the urethra. An α1-receptor antagonist prevents this contraction, producing a relaxed bladder neck and a dilated urethra.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine acts at cholinergic receptors, not the α1-adrenergic receptors that constrict the bladder neck.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dihydrotestosterone drives prostatic cellular proliferation, not acute α1-mediated smooth muscle contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitric oxide is a vasodilator relevant to PDE-5 inhibitor pharmacology, not an α1 agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandin E1 is not the ligand for α1-adrenergic receptors.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has urinary hesitancy and a weak stream. His physician explains that two processes narrow his prostatic urethra: cellular proliferation of the gland and α1-mediated smooth muscle tone. Which of the following best describes what an α1-blocker does to these two processes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contracts the detrusor to overcome the mechanical obstruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduces the gland size by inhibiting androgen synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relieves the smooth muscle contraction but does not reverse the proliferation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverses the cellular proliferation and relaxes the smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverses the cellular proliferation but does not affect smooth muscle tone

explanation.summary: α1-Blockers relieve the smooth-muscle (dynamic) component of BPH obstruction; they do not reverse the mechanical obstruction from cellular proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In BPH, cellular proliferation causes mechanical obstruction of the prostatic urethra, and α1-receptor activation in prostatic smooth muscle, the prostatic urethra, and the bladder neck adds smooth-muscle contraction that further decreases urine flow. Blocking these α1-receptors prevents the smooth muscle contraction, dilates the urethra, and decreases resistance to urine flow, but it does nothing to the proliferating tissue itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: α1-Blockers relax smooth muscle of the prostate, urethra, and bladder neck; they do not contract the detrusor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: α1-Blockers do not inhibit androgen synthesis or shrink the gland.
whyWrongByChoice.D: α1-Blockers do not reverse cellular proliferation; they act only on smooth muscle contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is reversed: α1-blockers affect smooth muscle tone and have no effect on proliferation.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is prescribed prazosin for hypertension. His physician warns him that he is most likely to experience dizziness or fainting on standing during a specific window of treatment. Which of the following is that window?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After 6 months, when receptor upregulation occurs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only during the first hour after each daily dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only when a dose is missed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first 24 hours after the first dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: The second week of therapy, once steady state is reached

explanation.summary: The risk of orthostatic hypotension with α1-blockers is highest within the first 24 hours of the first dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The risk of orthostatic hypotension is higher within the first 24 hours of the first dose of an α1-blocker. Prazosin's higher affinity for α1-receptors and rapid onset of action increase this risk, so patients should be counseled to rise slowly from sitting or supine positions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no described 6-month receptor upregulation window; risk is greatest with the first dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stated window is the first 24 hours after the first dose, not the first hour after every dose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Missing a dose is not the risk period; re-dosing after discontinuation is, because it recreates the first-dose situation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The peak risk is at initiation, not at steady state in the second week.

questions.stem: A pharmacy student is asked to identify an α1-adrenergic blocker from a list of drug names using the class's characteristic suffix. Which of the following is an α1-blocker?

explanation.summary: All α1-blocker drugs end with the suffix '-osin'.
explanation.whyCorrect: All α1-blocker drugs end with the suffix '-osin', as in prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin, alfuzosin, tamsulosin, and silodosin. Alfuzosin is a nonselective α1-blocker by receptor selectivity that is used uroselectively for BPH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Atenolol ends in '-olol' and is a β-blocker, not an α1-blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clonidine is an α2-agonist that blocks norepinephrine release in the CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metoprolol is a β-blocker; the '-olol' suffix marks β-blockade, not α1-blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, which can cause severe hypotension when combined with an α1-blocker.

questions.stem: A resident compares the two nonselective α-antagonists used in the initial management of pheochromocytoma before surgical resection. Which of the following properties distinguishes phenoxybenzamine from phentolamine?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phenoxybenzamine has a shorter duration of action

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenoxybenzamine is used for short-term hypertensive control
