whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the effect to airway smooth muscle and secretions, not pulmonary vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a sudden, frequent urge to urinate with occasional involuntary leakage, and urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity. She is started on oxybutynin. What is the mechanism by which this drug relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck and trigone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking muscarinic receptors to slow detrusor contractions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing urine production through a renal diuretic effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxing the internal urethral sphincter to ease voiding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating detrusor muscle contraction to empty the bladder

explanation.summary: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic that slows detrusor contractions to control urge incontinence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes oxybutynin as the prototypical anticholinergic for urinary incontinence (overactive bladder); by blocking M3 receptors it slows bladder detrusor contractions, helping patients control urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxybutynin is antimuscarinic, not an alpha-adrenergic blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drug does not increase urine production; it reduces involuntary bladder contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics reduce detrusor overactivity; they do not work by relaxing the urethral sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating detrusor contraction would worsen urgency and leakage.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupil to examine the retina during a funduscopic exam. Which of the following anticholinergic agents, administered as an eye drop, is most appropriate for producing mydriasis?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic drops such as tropicamide (or atropine) dilate the pupil for eye exams.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine and tropicamide drops are used to dilate the pupil for ophthalmoscopic exams; the mydriasis helps with retinal and pupillary examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate does not penetrate well and is not described as an ophthalmic mydriatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats overactive bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used as a transdermal patch for motion sickness, not as an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A toxicology instructor teaches the classic anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic. A poisoned patient who is described as 'mad as a hatter' is exhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased secretions, dry mouth, and thirst

explanation.summary: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to the CNS effects of anticholinergic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick maps 'mad as a hatter' to central nervous system effects such as drowsiness, hallucinations, and coma, which result from central muscarinic blockade in agents that penetrate the CNS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry mouth and decreased secretions correspond to 'dry as a bone'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushed skin corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis and blurred vision correspond to 'blind as a bat'.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tachycardia (and overheating) corresponds to 'hot as a hare'.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with severe lower abdominal pain and states he has not urinated in several days. He has no prior urinary problems and is generally healthy but recently began an over-the-counter allergy medicine for a runny nose. Examination reveals a markedly distended bladder requiring catheterization. Which property of his allergy medication best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains diphenhydramine with anticholinergic properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a direct cholinergic agonist that stimulates the detrusor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a diuretic that overfilled the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that relaxes the bladder neck

explanation.summary: OTC diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties that can cause urinary retention, especially in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case describes exactly this scenario: the allergy medicine contains diphenhydramine, an antihistamine with anticholinergic properties. By blocking muscarinic receptors it decreases detrusor contraction and causes urinary retention, a particular risk in elderly patients who also face confusion, constipation, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cholinergic agonist would promote urination, not cause retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A diuretic would increase urine output; the problem was inability to void due to anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor increases acetylcholine and cholinergic activity, opposite to what caused retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-blockade at the bladder neck would ease urine flow, not cause retention.

questions.stem: A patient who took a large amount of an anticholinergic agent is brought to the emergency department. On the anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic, the finding 'dry as a bone' reflects which underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone at M2 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cutaneous vasodilation in the skin vasculature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased gut motility with delayed transit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupillary dilation from iris sphincter blockade

explanation.summary: 'Dry as a bone' reflects inhibition of secretions, producing dry mouth, dry eyes, and decreased sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick attributes 'dry as a bone' to the general inhibition of secretions in mucous membranes and skin, giving dry mouth, dry eyes, and reduced sweating from muscarinic blockade of exocrine glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone produces tachycardia ('hot as a hare').
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous flushing corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased gut motility contributes to 'full as a flask' (retention/constipation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation corresponds to 'blind as a bat'.

questions.stem: A farm worker is brought in after exposure to an organophosphate insecticide, with copious secretions, bradycardia, and pinpoint pupils. Which anticholinergic drug is the appropriate antidote for this acetylcholine-excess (muscarinic) toxicity?

explanation.summary: Atropine is the antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, such as organophosphate or muscarine poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states atropine is an antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, including poisoning by organophosphates or muscarine-containing wild mushrooms. By competitively blocking muscarinic receptors, it reverses the excess-cholinergic secretions, bradycardia, and miosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin is a bladder-selective agent for overactive bladder, not a poisoning antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used for motion sickness, not as the antidote of choice for cholinergic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A student is asked to predict adverse effects of anticholinergic drugs from their receptor actions. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of an anticholinergic agent?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics decrease GI motility, which can lead to constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review question confirms constipation as a correct answer: anticholinergics inhibit gut smooth muscle contraction and decrease motility, which can cause constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They cause tachycardia by blocking vagal tone, not bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They decrease, not increase, GI motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease secretions, causing dry mouth, not increased salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They cause mydriasis (dilation), not miosis.

questions.stem: A neurologist notes that some antimuscarinic drugs are useful for CNS diseases while others are not, depending on how well they penetrate the brain. Which of the following best explains why ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are NOT useful in treating Parkinson disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are direct dopamine receptor antagonists in the striatum

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are rapidly metabolized in the gut wall before they are absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: They block nicotinic rather than muscarinic receptors in the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: They do not adequately cross into the central nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate rather than block muscarinic receptors centrally

explanation.summary: CNS penetration varies among antimuscarinics; poorly penetrating agents cannot treat central diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that muscarinic antagonists have variable CNS penetration. Certain agents (e.g., benztropine, atropine) carry greater CNS effects, whereas ipratropium and glycopyrrolate do not penetrate the CNS well and therefore are not useful in treating CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are antimuscarinics, not dopamine antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the difference to CNS penetration, not to pre-absorption metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs are muscarinic antagonists; the issue is CNS penetration, not a switch to nicotinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They block, rather than stimulate, muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked why a muscarinic antagonist blocks parasympathetic effects on smooth muscle but does not interrupt transmission at autonomic ganglia. Which of the following best describes the location of the receptors targeted by muscarinic antagonists?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Between first-order and second-order neurons of the autonomic nervous system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Between second-order parasympathetic neurons and their target organs

choices.label: D
choices.text: On presynaptic terminals of first-order sympathetic neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: On the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells

explanation.summary: Muscarinic receptors sit between second-order parasympathetic neurons and target organs; nicotinic receptors sit between first- and second-order autonomic neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that acetylcholine receptors are divided into nicotinic and muscarinic types. Nicotinic receptors are usually found between first-order and second-order neurons in the autonomic nervous system, whereas muscarinic receptors are typically found between second-order parasympathetic neurons and their target organs, such as smooth muscle. Muscarinic antagonists therefore act at the target organ, not the ganglion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle uses nicotinic receptors, not muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The synapse between first- and second-order autonomic neurons uses nicotinic receptors, which anticholinergics do not block.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic receptors are described on the target-organ side of second-order parasympathetic neurons, not on first-order sympathetic terminals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The adrenal medulla is not the site the brick identifies for muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the rest-and-digest functions of the parasympathetic nervous system in order to predict which effects an anticholinergic drug would oppose. Which of the following is a normal effect of parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dilation of the pupils by the radial dilator muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase in heart rate at the sinoatrial node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Opening of the urinary and gastrointestinal sphincters

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduction in sweat gland output and dry skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle with bronchodilation

explanation.summary: Parasympathetic stimulation opens urinary and GI sphincters, increases secretions and motility, slows the heart, and constricts pupils; anticholinergics oppose all of these.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the cholinergic effects as increasing glandular secretions (saliva, sweat, gastric, intestinal), increasing GI motility, opening urinary and GI sphincters, slowing the heart rate, and constricting pupils. These functions support eating and rejuvenating the body, in contrast to the fight-or-flight responses of the sympathetic system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic stimulation constricts the pupils; dilation (mydriasis) is an anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic stimulation slows the heart rate; tachycardia results from muscarinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergic stimulation increases sweat secretion; reduced sweating is an anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cholinergic activity at lung M3 receptors causes bronchoconstriction, not relaxation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man receives dilating eye drops before a retinal examination. Several hours later he reports that distant objects look normal but he cannot focus on the print of a magazine. Which of the following best explains this complaint?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constriction of the pupil limiting light entry

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased tear production drying the corneal surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased intraocular pressure compressing the optic nerve

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of accommodation by the lens

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic eye drops cause cycloplegia, a loss of lens accommodation that blurs near vision.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the head, ears, eyes, nose, and throat effects of muscarinic blockade as pupillary dilation causing photophobia and decreased ability of accommodation by the lens, resulting in blurred vision (cycloplegia). The summary notes that MAs are used as eye drops to induce both mydriasis and cycloplegia for ophthalmoscopic exams.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergic drops dilate rather than constrict the pupil.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased lacrimation causes dry eyes but does not selectively impair near focus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes blurred vision to cycloplegia, not to increased intraocular pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic blockade decreases, rather than causes spasm of, accommodation; the ciliary muscle is relaxed, not contracted.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after eating berries from a garden shrub. His temperature is 39.4 C, his skin is hot, dry, and flushed, and his pupils are widely dilated. Which of the following best explains his elevated body temperature?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased skeletal muscle heat production from tremor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of sweating with decreased heat dissipation

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic hyperthermia ('hot as a hare') results from blocked sweat secretion and decreased heat dissipation; the flushing ('red as a beet') follows the rising central temperature.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's integumentary effect of muscarinic blockade is inhibition of secretions causing reduced sweating, leading to decreased heat dissipation and thus skin flushing. The toxidrome mnemonic describes tachycardia and decreased heat dissipation leading to overheating (hot as a hare) and flushed skin that results from increasing central temperature (red as a beet). Plant-alkaloid anticholinergics such as atropine come from A. belladonna, a plant associated with severe poisoning.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The skin is flushed (vasodilated), not vasoconstricted; flushing follows the rising central temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is drug-induced overheating from blocked sweating, not a pyrogen-mediated fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes overheating to lost heat dissipation, not to muscle heat production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitochondrial uncoupling is not a mechanism of anticholinergic toxicity described in the brick.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company develops an experimental anticholinergic that, unlike most agents in the class, blocks M3 receptors but has no activity at M2 receptors. Compared with atropine, which of the following effects would this drug be expected to lack?

explanation.summary: Of the organ effects in the brick's table, only the cardiac effect (increased heart rate) is mediated by M2; every other listed effect is M3.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's anticholinergic effects table assigns M3 to the eyes, nasal glands, salivary glands, lungs, GI tract, urinary bladder, and skin, and assigns M2 only to the heart (increased heart rate). It also notes that most anticholinergics do not show selectivity for muscarinic subtypes, so an M3-selective agent would be unusual and would spare the M2-mediated cardiac effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased bronchial secretions are M3-mediated in the table.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Salivary gland dryness is an M3 effect and would still occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased sweating is listed as an M3 effect on the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased urination reflects M3 blockade in the bladder.

questions.stem: An anesthesiologist administers atropine to a 50-year-old woman shortly before induction of general anesthesia for an elective operation. Which of the following pairs of benefits best describes the rationale for this preoperative use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronchoconstriction with reduced pulmonary blood flow during induction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased respiratory secretions and reduced likelihood of bradycardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased gastric emptying and a lower risk of perioperative aspiration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lowered blood pressure and reduced bleeding in the surgical field

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preoperative sedation and reliable postoperative pain relief

explanation.summary: Atropine is given around surgery to dry respiratory secretions and to reduce the likelihood of bradycardia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine reduces respiratory secretions prior to the induction of anesthesia or surgical procedures, and its summary notes that many MAs, especially atropine, are used in surgery to decrease secretions and reduce the likelihood of bradycardia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscarinic blockade causes bronchodilation, not bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anticholinergics decrease GI motility; they do not speed gastric emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atropine raises heart rate through M2 blockade; lowering blood pressure or reducing bleeding is not a described purpose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Atropine is not used for sedation or analgesia; CNS effects such as drowsiness are adverse effects, not the goal.

questions.stem: A pharmacognosy lecture covers anticholinergic drugs that are obtained directly from plant alkaloids rather than by chemical synthesis. Which of the following pairs of drugs is naturally extracted from plants?

explanation.summary: Atropine and scopolamine are naturally extracted plant alkaloids.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that modern anticholinergics include atropine and scopolamine, which are both naturally extracted from plant alkaloids; atropine is named after A. belladonna, which itself is named for Atropos, the Fate who cut the thread of life.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Darifenacin and solifenacin are overactive-bladder agents, not natural plant alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ipratropium and tiotropium are inhaled agents, not the plant-derived alkaloids the brick names.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxybutynin and tolterodine are bladder agents that do not carry the 'trop' label and are not described as plant extracts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trihexyphenidyl is listed among agents lacking the 'trop' label; neither is described as plant-derived.

questions.stem: A student notices that many anticholinergic drug names contain the letters 'trop,' reminiscent of atropine. Which of the following anticholinergic drugs does NOT carry this 'trop' label in its name?

explanation.summary: Oxybutynin, trihexyphenidyl, and tolterodine are anticholinergics without the 'trop' naming cue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that many anticholinergics used clinically include 'trop' in their name, but that others, including oxybutynin, trihexyphenidyl, and tolterodine, do not carry the 'trop' label.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benztropine contains 'trop' and is a CNS-penetrating antimuscarinic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium contains 'trop' and is an inhaled anticholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tiotropium contains 'trop' and is an inhaled anticholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide contains 'trop' and is an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with urge incontinence and detrusor overactivity was started on oxybutynin but stopped it because of side effects. Her physician wants to prescribe a different agent with the same mechanism. Which of the following is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Tolterodine, darifenacin, solifenacin, and fesoterodine share oxybutynin's antimuscarinic action on the bladder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names oxybutynin as the prototypical anticholinergic for urinary incontinence and states that other agents with similar effects are tolterodine, darifenacin, solifenacin, and fesoterodine, all used in the management of urge incontinence and bladder detrusor overactivity by slowing bladder contractions (M3).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate is mentioned for its poor CNS penetration, not as an overactive-bladder agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Scopolamine is a transdermal patch for motion sickness and postsurgical nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tiotropium is an inhaled anticholinergic prescribed for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an eye drop used to dilate the pupil for ophthalmoscopic exams.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman reports sudden urges to urinate followed by involuntary loss of urine with no apparent trigger. Before starting medication, her physician reviews contributing factors. Which of the following is known to worsen this condition?

explanation.summary: Urge incontinence (overactive bladder) has no known cause, but caffeine, constipation, obesity, and diabetes make it worse.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that urge incontinence, sometimes called overactive bladder, involves a sudden urge to urinate followed by involuntary loss of urine for no apparent reason; the cause is unknown, but caffeine, constipation, obesity, and diabetes worsen the problem. Bladder training and pelvic floor exercises can help control urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diet protein content is not among the aggravating factors named.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation is not described as worsening overactive bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Exercise is not listed as an aggravating factor; the brick recommends pelvic floor exercises and bladder training as helpful measures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D supplementation is not described as worsening overactive bladder.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD asks his physician about an inhaled maintenance medication that works by blocking muscarinic receptors in the airways. Which of the following drugs is an inhaled anticholinergic used for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Ipratropium and tiotropium are the inhaled anticholinergics for asthma and COPD.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that anticholinergics such as ipratropium and tiotropium are prescribed for patients with asthma and COPD to reduce mucus secretions and decrease bronchoconstriction and airway resistance, and that they are also formulated in combination with beta-agonists and corticosteroids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fesoterodine is another overactive-bladder agent, not an inhaled drug.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Solifenacin is used for urge incontinence and detrusor overactivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trihexyphenidyl is a non-'trop' anticholinergic not used by inhalation for airway disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A geriatrician explains to residents why an antihistamine dose that is well tolerated by a 30-year-old can cause confusion, urinary retention, and falls in an 80-year-old. Which of the following best accounts for the increased susceptibility of elderly patients to anticholinergic effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster hepatic conversion to active metabolites

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fewer cholinergic receptor cells and slower drug elimination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greater blood-brain barrier exclusion of the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased acetylcholine release compensating for blockade

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of cholinergic receptors with age

explanation.summary: Elderly patients have a decrease in cholinergic receptor cells and slower drug elimination, raising their risk of confusion, urinary retention, constipation, and falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case conclusion, medications with anticholinergic properties are described as especially problematic in elderly people because they have a decrease in cholinergic receptor cells and a slower drug elimination, which puts them at high risk of confusion, urinary retention, constipation, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick cites slower elimination, not faster metabolic activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Greater exclusion from the brain would reduce, not increase, CNS effects such as confusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased acetylcholine release would offset blockade rather than heighten sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes a decrease, not an increase, in cholinergic receptor cells with age.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with urge incontinence asks whether she can take the same bladder medication her 40-year-old daughter uses. Her physician agrees to prescribe it only with careful monitoring. Which of the following adverse effects is the primary reason for this caution in her age group?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics for urinary incontinence should be avoided or carefully monitored in patients older than 65 because of increased constipation risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that anticholinergics can cause urinary retention and constipation in the elderly, and that for drugs used for urinary incontinence, use in elderly patients (>65 years old) should be avoided if possible or carefully monitored due to increased risk of constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergics raise, not lower, heart rate through M2 blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anticholinergics slow GI motility; diarrhea is a cholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease secretions, producing dry mouth rather than excessive salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blood pressure effects are not the concern the brick raises for antimuscarinic bladder drugs in the elderly.

questions.stem: Two patients are evaluated for suspected anticholinergic toxicity. Patient 1 has dilated pupils, dry skin, decreased sweating, and decreased urination. Patient 2 has the same peripheral findings plus new hallucinations and fluctuating attention. Which of the following statements about these presentations is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both presentations carry equal concern because the toxidrome is a fixed set of findings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient 1 requires urgent antidote therapy whereas Patient 2 can be observed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient 1's findings are more concerning because peripheral signs indicate a larger ingested dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient 2's central findings are more concerning and point toward chronic toxicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patient 2's findings exclude anticholinergic toxicity because hallucinations are not part of the toxidrome

explanation.summary: Central findings (delirium, hallucinations) are more concerning than isolated peripheral findings and point toward chronic anticholinergic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the presentation of toxidrome signs depends on the kinetics of the agent. Peripheral findings of mydriasis, dry skin, decreased sweating, and decreased urination alone are less concerning, whereas central findings such as delirium and hallucinations, alone or with peripheral findings, are more concerning and point toward chronic toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although the toxidrome encompasses all the clinical features, the brick states that presentation varies with kinetics and that central findings carry greater concern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The patient with central findings is the more concerning one; the brick does not suggest observation for central toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick describes isolated peripheral findings as less concerning, not as markers of a larger dose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hallucinations, drowsiness, and coma are explicitly part of the anticholinergic toxidrome ('mad as a hatter').

questions.stem: During an emergency medicine rotation, a student hears the attending describe a patient as having 'a classic toxidrome.' Which of the following best defines this term as used in clinical practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A collection of exam and diagnostic findings that may result from a poison

choices.label: B
choices.text: A genetic syndrome that predisposes a patient to severe adverse drug reactions

choices.label: C
choices.text: A laboratory panel that identifies the specific toxin present in serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: The specific antidote regimen matched to a given class of poisons

choices.label: E
choices.text: The dose of a drug above which toxicity is guaranteed to occur

explanation.summary: A toxidrome is a collection of findings, from physical exam or ancillary testing, that may result from a poison; it narrows the differential but has exceptions and limitations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that physicians, especially in the ER, use the word 'toxidrome' to mean a collection of findings, either from the physical examination or from ancillary diagnostic testing, that may result from any poison or toxin. Numerous toxidromes are defined in the medical literature, and although they help narrow the differential diagnosis, caution must be exercised to recognize the exceptions and limitations of each.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The term refers to findings caused by a poison, not an inherited predisposition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A toxidrome is a pattern of findings, not a serum toxin assay.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A toxidrome is diagnostic pattern recognition, not a treatment regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A toxidrome describes a clinical picture, not a threshold dose.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of an anticholinergic drug. He has not urinated in 14 hours, has absent bowel sounds, and has had no bowel movement. Which element of the classic anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic do these findings represent?

explanation.summary: 'Full as a flask' describes decreased excretion of both urine and stool due to decreased motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's mnemonic assigns 'full as a flask' to the decreased excretion of wastes, both urine and stool, that results from decreased motility under muscarinic blockade; the toxidrome figure likewise shows urinary retention and absent bowel sounds.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 'Blind as a bat' refers to mydriasis, photophobia, and cycloplegia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 'Hot as a hare' refers to tachycardia and overheating from decreased heat dissipation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to CNS effects such as drowsiness, hallucinations, and coma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 'Red as a beet' refers to flushed skin from rising central temperature.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with irritable bowel syndrome has frequent loose stools with crampy abdominal pain. Her physician prescribes a muscarinic antagonist. Which of the following effects of the drug is responsible for improving her diarrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of vagal afferent pain fibers from the intestinal wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced secretion of protective intestinal mucus by goblet cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased absorption of water and sodium by the colonic mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxation of intestinal smooth muscle with decreased motility

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of intestinal sphincter opening with faster transit

explanation.summary: Muscarinic antagonists relax GI smooth muscle and slow motility, which is useful for diarrhea, especially in irritable bowel syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's GI effect of muscarinic blockade is inhibition of smooth muscle contraction with decreased motility, and its summary states that MAs help relax excretory muscles and are thus useful in treating urge incontinence of the bladder and diarrhea, especially in irritable bowel syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mechanism is smooth muscle relaxation at muscarinic receptors, not blockade of afferent pain fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticholinergics inhibit, rather than enhance, GI mucus output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the antidiarrheal benefit to decreased motility, not to altered mucosal water absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sphincter opening is a cholinergic effect; anticholinergics oppose it.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease has troublesome tremor, and his neurologist wishes to add a muscarinic antagonist that acts within the central nervous system. Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Benztropine is a CNS-penetrating muscarinic antagonist, in contrast to ipratropium and glycopyrrolate, which cannot treat CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that MAs have vastly variable CNS penetration, which is why certain MAs such as benztropine and atropine are associated with greater CNS effects, while agents such as ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are not useful in treating CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease. Benztropine is also listed among the important muscarinic antagonists to know.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycopyrrolate is named specifically as an agent not useful for CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ipratropium does not penetrate the CNS well and is used for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tiotropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolterodine is used for urge incontinence and detrusor overactivity.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has persistent nausea in the recovery room after a laparoscopic operation. The anesthesiologist applies a medication formulated as a transdermal patch. Which of the following drugs was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine (hyoscine) patches treat postsurgical nausea as well as motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that scopolamine (hyoscine) is usually formulated as a transdermal patch and is used to treat motion sickness and postsurgical nausea; the anticholinergic effects table also lists decreased vomiting among the GI effects of muscarinic blockade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate is noted for its poor CNS penetration; it is not the transdermal antiemetic patch described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats urinary incontinence, not postoperative nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an eye drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man required bladder catheterization for acute urinary retention caused by an over-the-counter diphenhydramine allergy pill. After his symptoms resolve, which of the following is the most appropriate discharge plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apply a scopolamine patch for his runny nose instead

choices.label: B
choices.text: Call for advice before any OTC medication and return in 2 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase daily fluid intake to keep the bladder flushed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resume the allergy pill at half the dose and recheck in 6 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start scheduled oxybutynin to prevent recurrence of retention

explanation.summary: Elderly patients should seek advice before taking OTC medications with anticholinergic properties, with close follow-up after an episode of retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case conclusion, after identifying diphenhydramine as the cause, the physician tells NK to call for advice before taking any over-the-counter medication and arranges a follow-up visit in 2 days, because elderly patients are at high risk of confusion, urinary retention, constipation, and falls from anticholinergic drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Scopolamine is another anticholinergic and is used for motion sickness and postsurgical nausea, not rhinorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The retention was due to muscarinic blockade of the bladder, not to inadequate fluid intake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Continuing the offending anticholinergic antihistamine risks recurrent retention; the brick advises seeking advice before OTC use, not a dose reduction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxybutynin is itself an anticholinergic that decreases detrusor contraction and would worsen, not prevent, urinary retention.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman taking an oral antimuscarinic for overactive bladder reports that her eyes feel gritty and irritated and that she now needs lubricating drops. Which of the following best explains this adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conjunctival vasoconstriction from blockade of nicotinic receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corneal edema from blockade of M2 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased lacrimation from blockade of M3 receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased lacrimation from stimulation of M2 receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupillary constriction from stimulation of M3 receptors

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinics decrease lacrimation via M3 blockade, causing dry eyes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's anticholinergic effects table lists the eye effects as mydriasis and decreased lacrimation mediated by M3 receptors, and the text notes that inhibition of secretions leads to dry eyes and dry mouth. Systemic antimuscarinics lack subtype selectivity, so a bladder drug also dries the eyes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most anticholinergics do not block nicotinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heart, not the eye, is the M2-mediated organ in the brick's table, and corneal edema is not a described effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease, not increase, tear secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimuscarinics block rather than stimulate M3 receptors and cause mydriasis, not constriction.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is admitted with dizziness and an ECG showing impaired conduction through the atrioventricular node with a slow ventricular rate. Which of the following anticholinergic drugs is indicated to improve cardiac conduction in this setting?

explanation.summary: Atropine improves cardiac conduction in sinus bradycardia and atrioventricular node block.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine, the oldest and most established anticholinergic, improves cardiac conduction in sinus bradycardia and atrioventricular node block by inhibiting M2-mediated parasympathetic slowing of the heart.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Darifenacin is an overactive-bladder agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats urge incontinence and detrusor overactivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tiotropium is an inhaled agent for asthma and COPD, not a cardiac drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with asthma is accidentally exposed to a drug that activates M3 receptors throughout the body. Which of the following pulmonary changes would be expected, and what is the corresponding rationale for treating asthma with inhaled muscarinic antagonists?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bronchoconstriction with increased mucus; antagonists lower airway resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronchodilation with decreased mucus; antagonists reverse excessive airway relaxation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased surfactant; antagonists restore alveolar stability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paralysis of the diaphragm; antagonists restore neuromuscular transmission

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary vasodilation; antagonists restore ventilation-perfusion matching

explanation.summary: M3 activation in the lungs causes bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; blocking it with inhaled antagonists reduces airway resistance in asthma and COPD.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick recalls that the presence of M3 receptors in the lungs can cause bronchoconstriction, and that anticholinergics such as ipratropium and tiotropium reduce mucus secretions and decrease bronchoconstriction and airway resistance, allowing easier respiration in asthma and COPD.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchodilation and decreased mucus are the effects of muscarinic blockade, not of M3 activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Surfactant production is not a muscarinic effect described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle driven by nicotinic receptors, which muscarinic agents and antagonists do not affect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes airway smooth muscle and secretion effects, not pulmonary vascular effects.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl receives tropicamide drops for a dilated eye examination. On leaving the clinic into bright sunlight she squints, complains that the light hurts her eyes, and asks for sunglasses. Which of the following best explains her symptom?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corneal abrasion from the drop's preservative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess light entry through the dilated pupil

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of tear film from decreased lacrimation

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic mydriasis produces photophobia because the dilated pupil cannot limit light entry.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists pupillary dilation (mydriasis) causing photophobia as a head, ears, eyes, nose, and throat effect of muscarinic blockade, and the toxidrome mnemonic groups mydriasis, photophobia, and cycloplegia together as 'blind as a bat.'

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes light sensitivity to mydriasis, not to corneal injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intraocular pressure is not the mechanism the brick gives for photophobia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conjunctival inflammation is not a described effect of tropicamide drops.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Decreased lacrimation causes dry eyes, but the light-triggered pain is due to the dilated pupil.

questions.stem: A toxicologist is classifying several cholinesterase inhibitors by their mechanism of enzyme binding. Which of the following agents irreversibly phosphorylates the acetylcholinesterase enzyme?

explanation.summary: Organophosphates such as malathion irreversibly phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malathion is an organophosphate, the class of irreversible indirect-acting cholinomimetics. These agents phosphorylate the AChE enzyme, and the phosphorylated complex can undergo aging that makes inhibition essentially permanent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Edrophonium is a very short-acting reversible inhibitor used to diagnose myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neostigmine is a reversible carbamate inhibitor that carbamoylates AChE, a process that can restore enzyme function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physostigmine is a reversible AChE inhibitor, not an organophosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyridostigmine is a reversible inhibitor used in myasthenia gravis, not an irreversible one.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anticholinergic toxicity is developing central symptoms including delirium and agitation. Which of the following cholinesterase inhibitors is able to cross the blood-brain barrier to reverse these central effects?

explanation.summary: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that crosses the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Physostigmine is a tertiary (3 degree) amine, so it crosses the blood-brain barrier and can reverse both peripheral and central symptoms of anticholinergic toxicity, which is why it is the antidote for atropine overdose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Edrophonium is used to diagnose myasthenia gravis and does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Malathion is a toxic organophosphate insecticide, not a therapeutic antidote for anticholinergic toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neostigmine is a quaternary amine and cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyridostigmine likewise does not cross the blood-brain barrier.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to name a drug that raises synaptic acetylcholine by reversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, rather than by binding acetylcholine receptors directly. Which of the following is the best example?

explanation.summary: Neostigmine is an indirect-acting reversible AChE inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics inhibit the breakdown of acetylcholine by cholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. Neostigmine is a reversible carbamate inhibitor and a classic example of this indirect mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bethanechol is a direct-acting agent that binds acetylcholine receptors directly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbachol is a direct-acting cholinomimetic, not an enzyme inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting agonist at muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarin inhibits acetylcholinesterase but does so irreversibly, not reversibly.

questions.stem: A farm worker is brought to the emergency department after heavy exposure to an organophosphate insecticide. The physician administers pralidoxime (2-PAM). Which of the following best describes the primary function of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accelerates aging of the enzyme-inhibitor complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds and blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly blocks nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal

explanation.summary: Pralidoxime is an oxime reactivator that regenerates acetylcholinesterase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pralidoxime binds a separate site on AChE and, acting as a strong nucleophile, can displace the organophosphate and break the phosphorus-enzyme bond, regenerating normal cholinesterase function if given before aging occurs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pralidoxime prevents aging rather than accelerating it; aging makes reactivation impossible.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking muscarinic receptors is the action of atropine, not pralidoxime.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pralidoxime does not block nicotinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pralidoxime does not affect acetylcholine release; it restores enzyme function.

questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with physostigmine overdose and develops signs of excessive cholinergic stimulation. Which of the following is the most appropriate reversal agent?

explanation.summary: Atropine, an antimuscarinic agent, reverses excess cholinergic stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atropine is a competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. By blocking these receptors it counteracts the muscarinic effects of excess acetylcholine, making it the reversal agent for a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor overdose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Donepezil is itself a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen the toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malathion is a toxic organophosphate that would add to cholinergic excess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neostigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor and would aggravate the overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic agonist and would intensify, not reverse, the symptoms.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man accidentally receives an overdose of neostigmine. On examination, which of the following ocular findings is most likely?

explanation.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitor excess causes miosis (pupillary constriction).
explanation.whyCorrect: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, and stimulation of these receptors in the eye causes constriction of the pupillary sphincter muscle, producing miosis and increased lacrimation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cycloplegia results from blocking muscarinic tone, not from cholinergic excess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic stimulation increases, rather than decreases, lacrimation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis (pupil dilation) results from antimuscarinic or sympathetic activity, the opposite of excess acetylcholine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A dilated pupil is an antimuscarinic effect and is not expected with cholinergic excess.

questions.stem: A neurologist suspects myasthenia gravis in a 32-year-old woman with fluctuating ptosis and diplopia. A very short-acting cholinesterase inhibitor is given, and her symptoms briefly improve, confirming the diagnosis. Which of the following agents was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Edrophonium is a short-acting inhibitor used to confirm myasthenia gravis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edrophonium is a short-acting drug lasting 5 to 15 minutes that briefly improves the symptoms of myasthenia gravis, where acetylcholine stimulation is lacking at end organs, thereby confirming the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donepezil is used symptomatically in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridostigmine has a longer duration and is used to treat, rather than diagnose, myasthenia gravis; neostigmine is used for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physostigmine is used to treat atropine overdose, not to diagnose myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rivastigmine is used in dementia, not for diagnosing myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child ingests a plant containing atropine and develops dry, flushed skin, delirium, and tachycardia. Physostigmine is chosen as the antidote. Which property of physostigmine makes it especially suitable for treating this anticholinergic toxicity?

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a quaternary amine confined to the periphery

explanation.summary: Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity because it crosses the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Physostigmine is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor that replenishes acetylcholine in the synapse. Because it crosses the blood-brain barrier, it is effective in treating both the peripheral and central symptoms of anticholinergic toxicity such as delirium and agitation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Physostigmine raises acetylcholine by inhibiting its breakdown, not by blocking muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physostigmine is a reversible inhibitor, not an irreversible phosphorylating organophosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine; quaternary neostigmine is confined to the periphery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivating acetylcholinesterase is the role of pralidoxime, not physostigmine.

questions.stem: A soldier is exposed to the nerve agent sarin, and the phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase complex undergoes a process that strengthens the phosphorus-enzyme bond, making it stable and resistant to reactivation. Which of the following best describes this process, and its clinical implication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aging, after which oxime reactivators can no longer break the bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allosteric activation, which increases enzyme turnover

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbamoylation, which allows spontaneous enzyme recovery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competitive inhibition, which is easily reversed by acetylcholine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrolysis, which restores normal enzyme function

explanation.summary: Aging strengthens the phosphorus-enzyme bond and prevents reactivation.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the organophosphate binds, aging strengthens the phosphorus-enzyme bond. Once aging has occurred the enzyme-inhibitor complex is more stable and difficult to break even with oxime reactivators, so pralidoxime must be given before aging. For sarin, aging occurs within about 10 minutes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aging inactivates the enzyme; it does not allosterically activate it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbamoylation describes reversible carbamate inhibitors, not the aging of organophosphates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organophosphate inhibition is essentially irreversible, not easily reversed competitive inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hydrolysis in this setting contributes to aging, which strengthens rather than restores the enzyme.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man who sprays pesticides on his farm presents with breathlessness, excessive sweating, drooling, diarrhea, pinpoint pupils, and a heart rate of 46 beats per minute. Which of the following best explains this constellation of findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of muscarinic receptors by an antimuscarinic toxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Depletion of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Histamine release from mast cell degranulation

explanation.summary: Organophosphate poisoning causes cholinergic excess, summarized by DUMBBELLSS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exposure to organophosphate pesticides inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates and overstimulates muscarinic receptors. This produces the DUMBBELLSS toxidrome (diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchoconstriction, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating), matching this patient's findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-adrenergic overstimulation would cause tachycardia, not bradycardia and miosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes dry skin, dilated pupils, and tachycardia, the opposite of this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Symptoms are due to too much, not too little, acetylcholine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine release does not produce miosis, bradycardia, and the cholinergic secretory pattern seen here.

questions.stem: In managing severe organophosphate poisoning, atropine is administered together with pralidoxime. Which of the following best explains why atropine alone cannot fully treat this poisoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atropine agonizes muscarinic receptors and worsens symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atropine cannot restore the function of acetylcholinesterase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atropine reactivates the enzyme but not before aging occurs

explanation.summary: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but cannot regenerate the inhibited enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist that reverses muscarinic symptoms, but it cannot restore the function of the phosphorylated AChE enzyme. Because irreversible inhibition persists, atropine cannot be the only agent and is paired with pralidoxime, which regenerates the enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine antagonizes, rather than agonizes, muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Atropine does not bind acetylcholinesterase; it blocks muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atropine blocks muscarinic, not nicotinic, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivating the enzyme is pralidoxime's role, not atropine's.

questions.stem: A patient with open-angle glaucoma is treated with neostigmine. Which of the following best describes how this drug lowers intraocular pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks muscarinic receptors in the ciliary body

choices.label: B
choices.text: It causes mydriasis that opens the drainage angle

choices.label: C
choices.text: It decreases production of aqueous humor by dilating the pupil

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reduces resistance to aqueous humor outflow

explanation.summary: Neostigmine manages glaucoma by reducing resistance to aqueous humor outflow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neostigmine is used to manage glaucoma by reducing resistance to aqueous humor outflow, a mechanism similar to that of the direct-acting agents carbachol and pilocarpine, thereby lowering intraocular pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neostigmine increases cholinergic activity by inhibiting AChE; it does not block muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neostigmine causes miosis, not mydriasis; its benefit is reduced outflow resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It works by improving outflow, and cholinergic stimulation causes miosis, not pupil dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is a different drug class and is not neostigmine's mechanism.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing has her diagnosis of myasthenia gravis confirmed by a brief response to a short-acting cholinesterase inhibitor. Which of the following agents is most appropriate for her ongoing treatment?

explanation.summary: Pyridostigmine, with its longer duration of action, is used to treat myasthenia gravis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edrophonium and pyridostigmine are both used in myasthenia gravis, where acetylcholine stimulation is lacking at end organs. Edrophonium is short-acting (5-15 minutes) and only confirms the diagnosis, whereas pyridostigmine has a longer duration and can be used for treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist used to reverse cholinergic toxicity; it would not increase acetylcholine stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Edrophonium lasts only 5-15 minutes and is used to confirm the diagnosis, not for ongoing treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malathion is an irreversible organophosphate insecticide and is not a therapeutic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pralidoxime is an oxime reactivator for organophosphate poisoning, not a treatment for myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist studies how neostigmine interacts with acetylcholinesterase at the molecular level. Which of the following best describes this interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds acetylcholine receptors on the target cell directly

choices.label: C
choices.text: It carbamoylates the enzyme in a reversible process

choices.label: D
choices.text: It displaces bound inhibitor from a separate site on the enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: It phosphorylates the enzyme and the complex undergoes aging

explanation.summary: Reversible cholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine carbamoylate AChE.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neostigmine, physostigmine, and pyridostigmine are reversible AChE inhibitors that carbamoylate the enzyme. This carbamoylation is a reversible process that can restore enzyme function, in contrast to the phosphorylation produced by organophosphates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding acetylcholine receptors directly is the mechanism of direct-acting cholinomimetics like pilocarpine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive blockade of muscarinic receptors is the action of atropine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Displacing the organophosphate from the enzyme is the role of the oxime reactivator pralidoxime.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphorylation followed by aging describes irreversible organophosphates such as malathion, not neostigmine.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with Alzheimer disease is started on donepezil. His family asks what benefit they should expect from the medication. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It halts progression of the disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: It improves prognosis without affecting cognition

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may slightly improve cognition for short periods

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents the development of dementia in relatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reverses the underlying neuronal loss

explanation.summary: Donepezil may slightly improve cognition for short periods but does not change the course of dementia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Donepezil and rivastigmine are used to treat Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease. How they work in these disorders is not well understood, but they are cholinesterase inhibitors. The drugs do not change the course or prognosis of the dementia but may slightly improve cognition for short periods.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These drugs do not change the course of the dementia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The opposite is true: prognosis is unchanged while cognition may improve slightly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no preventive role for donepezil in family members.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Donepezil does not reverse the disease process; it only produces modest symptomatic benefit.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with drooping eyelids, double vision, and difficulty swallowing and talking that worsen through the day. Her symptoms improve with pyridostigmine. Which of the following best describes the underlying cause of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excessive presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible phosphorylation of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of muscarinic receptors on the skeletal muscle end plate membrane

explanation.summary: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition with autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myasthenia gravis is characterized by the presence of autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, so acetylcholine stimulation is lacking at end organs. This produces skeletal muscle weakness including drooping eyelids, double vision, and difficulty swallowing and talking. Cholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine improve symptoms by raising synaptic acetylcholine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The autoantibodies target the acetylcholine receptor, not the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myasthenia gravis involves too little acetylcholine stimulation at end organs, not excessive release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Irreversible AChE phosphorylation describes organophosphate poisoning, which causes cholinergic excess rather than weakness from receptor loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The receptors affected are the nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing, advanced myasthenia gravis is admitted with worsening weakness. Which of the following complications poses the greatest immediate threat to his life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma with permanent loss of vision

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemic cardiac arrest

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delirium from central cholinergic deficiency with aspiration of secretions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory muscle dysfunction with pneumonia and respiratory failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ventricular arrhythmia from autonomic involvement and sudden cardiac death

explanation.summary: Advanced myasthenia gravis can cause respiratory muscle dysfunction leading to fatal pneumonia and respiratory failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myasthenia gravis leads to skeletal muscle weakness. In advanced cases, the disease may cause respiratory muscle dysfunction, leading to fatal pneumonia and respiratory failure, which is the most dangerous complication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glaucoma is a condition treated with cholinesterase inhibitors, not a complication of myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rhabdomyolysis and kidney injury are not described features of myasthenia gravis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The disease affects nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction and does not produce central delirium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myasthenia gravis is a disorder of skeletal muscle weakness, not a cause of ventricular arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A medicinal chemist explains why organophosphorus compounds are such potent inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase. Which of the following structural features best accounts for this property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A carbamate ester linkage that is only slowly hydrolyzed by the active site serine

choices.label: B
choices.text: A planar aromatic ring that stacks and intercalates within the enzyme's active site gorge

choices.label: C
choices.text: A quaternary ammonium group closely resembling the choline moiety of acetylcholine

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tertiary amine that allows rapid passage into the central nervous system compartment

choices.label: E
choices.text: A tetrahedral configuration resembling the transition state of carboxyl ester hydrolysis

explanation.summary: Organophosphorus inhibitors are tetrahedral, resembling the transition state of carboxyl ester hydrolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Organophosphorus inhibitors are tetrahedral in configuration, a configuration that resembles the transition state formed in carboxyl ester hydrolysis. This mimicry of the enzyme's natural transition state underlies their tight, irreversible phosphorylation of AChE.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbamate esters describe reversible inhibitors such as neostigmine, which carbamoylate the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Organophosphates act through a tetrahedral phosphorus center, not a planar intercalating ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A quaternary ammonium group is a feature of neostigmine and pyridostigmine, not the basis of organophosphate inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tertiary amine character explains physostigmine's blood-brain barrier penetration, not organophosphate potency.

questions.stem: Soldiers are exposed to the nerve agent soman during a chemical attack. The medical team emphasizes that pralidoxime must be administered extremely rapidly. Approximately how long after exposure does aging of the enzyme-inhibitor complex occur with this agent?

explanation.summary: With soman, aging occurs in about 10 minutes, so oxime therapy must be nearly immediate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Organophosphates such as sarin and soman used in chemical warfare have very short aging times; with soman, aging occurs in 10 minutes. Because pralidoxime can only regenerate the enzyme if given before aging, the window for effective oxime therapy after soman exposure is extremely brief.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Even one hour exceeds the roughly 10-minute aging time of soman.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six hours is much longer than the very short aging time of chemical warfare agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aging with soman occurs far sooner than 24 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 72 hours vastly overestimates the aging time of soman.

questions.stem: Which of the following organophosphates is a neurotoxic gas that has been used as a chemical agent to poison populations during recent wars?

explanation.summary: Sarin is a neurotoxic organophosphate gas used in chemical warfare.
explanation.whyCorrect: Organophosphates such as sarin, soman, and VX are used in chemical warfare and can be extremely dangerous upon exposure. Sarin in particular is a neurotoxic gas that has been used as a chemical agent to poison populations during recent wars.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Malathion is an organophosphate insecticide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parathion is an organophosphate used as an insecticide on farms, not a warfare gas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physostigmine is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor used as an antidote for atropine overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pralidoxime is the oxime reactivator used to treat organophosphate poisoning.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old farm worker develops severe cholinergic toxicity after spraying parathion. He denies ingesting anything and wore a mask, but his clothing was soaked with the pesticide. Which pharmacokinetic property of organophosphates best explains his poisoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are unable to cross lipid membranes

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are very lipid-soluble and well absorbed through the skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are water-soluble quaternary amines confined to the plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have a low volume of distribution limited to the bloodstream

choices.label: E
choices.text: They require oral ingestion to be absorbed

explanation.summary: Organophosphates are very lipid-soluble and well absorbed from the skin, lungs, and gut.
explanation.whyCorrect: The organophosphates are well absorbed from the skin, lungs, gut, and other routes. In general, they are very lipid-soluble and have a high volume of distribution, which makes them effective insecticides but also very dangerous to humans, so dermal contact alone can cause serious toxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Their high lipid solubility means they cross lipid membranes readily.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Quaternary amine character describes neostigmine and pyridostigmine; organophosphates are lipid-soluble.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organophosphates have a high volume of distribution, not a low one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Organophosphates are absorbed through the skin and lungs, not only the gut.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with organophosphate poisoning has a heart rate of 45 beats per minute. Activation of which of the following receptor subtypes is most directly responsible for this finding?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: Cholinergic bradycardia is mediated by M2 muscarinic receptors in the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the clinically important muscarinic receptors (M1-M3), the effect of acetylcholine on the heart is decreased heart rate mediated by the M2 receptor. Excess acetylcholine from cholinesterase inhibition therefore produces bradycardia through M2 activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors are sympathetic and are not activated by acetylcholine excess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M1 receptors are not the subtype responsible for the cardiac effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors mediate the effects on eyes, glands, lungs, GI tract, bladder, and skin, not the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptor activation causes muscle fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis, not bradycardia.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old farm worker with parathion exposure is in considerable respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute and requires oxygen. Which of the following best explains his respiratory symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor blockade in airway smooth muscle causing bronchospasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronchoconstriction with increased bronchial secretions via M3 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased bronchial secretions via M3 receptors causing airway drying

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histamine release from pulmonary mast cells producing airway wall edema

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary vasodilation from M3 muscarinic receptors on pulmonary vessels

explanation.summary: Cholinergic stimulation of the lungs causes bronchoconstriction and bronchorrhea via M3 receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stimulating the parasympathetic nervous system in the lungs produces bronchoconstriction and bronchorrhea (increased bronchial secretions), mediated by M3 receptors. In cholinesterase inhibitor poisoning, dyspnea results from bronchoconstriction, increased bronchial secretions, and bronchospasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2 receptors are adrenergic and are not blocked by cholinesterase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholinergic excess increases, rather than decreases, bronchial secretions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine release from mast cells is not part of the cholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vasculature is not normally innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system, so muscarinic vasodilation is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient poisoned with an organophosphate insecticide develops widespread muscle twitching followed by weakness. Overstimulation of which of the following receptor types accounts for these findings?

explanation.summary: Muscle fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis are nicotinic effects of cholinergic excess.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to the muscarinic DUMBBELLSS effects, activation of nicotinic receptors by excess acetylcholine can cause muscle fasciculations (twitching) due to constant nicotinic activation, followed by weakness and paralysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors are not stimulated by acetylcholine accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M1 receptors are not responsible for skeletal muscle fasciculations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M2 receptors mediate decreased heart rate, not skeletal muscle effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors mediate glandular, smooth muscle, and pupillary effects, not skeletal muscle twitching.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man receiving neostigmine develops bradycardia, yet his blood pressure remains stable and no vasodilation is observed. Which of the following best explains the absence of vasodilation with this indirect-acting cholinomimetic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbamoylation of the enzyme spares vascular cholinesterase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neostigmine blocks muscarinic receptors on vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neostigmine is a quaternary amine that cannot reach the vasculature

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reflex sympathetic activation increases heart rate to offset vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vasculature is not normally innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system

explanation.summary: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics do not cause vasodilation because the vasculature lacks parasympathetic innervation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics raise acetylcholine only where it is released from cholinergic nerves. Because the vasculature is not normally innervated by the parasympathetic nervous system, these agents do not cause vasodilation. Instead they may lead to bradycardia with reflex vasoconstriction to maintain a steady cardiac output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbamoylation inhibits cholinesterase wherever the drug reaches; the explanation is the lack of parasympathetic innervation of vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine by inhibiting its breakdown; it does not block muscarinic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Being a quaternary amine limits blood-brain barrier crossing, not access to blood vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The compensatory response is reflex vasoconstriction to maintain cardiac output, not an increase in heart rate; the drug causes bradycardia.

questions.stem: A toxicologist compares toxic exposures to several cholinesterase inhibitors. Exposure to which of the following agents is expected to produce the most pronounced cholinergic adverse effects?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic adverse effects are more pronounced with the irreversible AChE inhibitors (organophosphates).
explanation.whyCorrect: Both reversible and irreversible cholinergics exaggerate the body's parasympathetic response, but the adverse effects are more pronounced with the irreversible AChE inhibitors such as organophosphates. Parathion is an organophosphate insecticide that irreversibly phosphorylates the enzyme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donepezil is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor used in dementia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Edrophonium is a very short-acting reversible inhibitor lasting only 5-15 minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neostigmine is a reversible carbamate inhibitor, so its effects are less pronounced than those of organophosphates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyridostigmine is a reversible inhibitor used to treat myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: Two patients present with cholinergic toxicity: one after an overdose of physostigmine and one after heavy exposure to parathion. Both receive atropine as the only treatment. In which patient is atropine expected to be more effective, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both equally, because atropine restores cholinesterase activity in each

choices.label: B
choices.text: The parathion patient, because atropine regenerates phosphorylated enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: The parathion patient, because organophosphates are more lipid-soluble

choices.label: D
choices.text: The physostigmine patient, because atropine reverses carbamoylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The physostigmine patient, because the enzyme inhibition is reversible

explanation.summary: Atropine is more effective in toxicity from reversible AChE inhibitors because it only blocks receptors while the reversible inhibition wears off.
explanation.whyCorrect: Atropine, a competitive antagonist of muscarinic receptors, blocks excessive acetylcholine from activating receptors until the agent has been excreted. It is more effective in toxicity caused by reversible AChE inhibitors such as physostigmine. Because atropine cannot restore the function of the AChE enzyme, it cannot be the only agent for toxicity from irreversible inhibitors, where pralidoxime must be added.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine does not restore cholinesterase activity in either case.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atropine cannot regenerate the enzyme; that is the role of pralidoxime.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipid solubility of organophosphates makes them more dangerous, not more responsive to atropine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atropine acts at muscarinic receptors and has no effect on carbamoylation of the enzyme.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a symptomatic arrhythmia and a heart rate of 38 beats per minute is given atropine, and his heart rate rises. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which atropine produced this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive blockade of nicotinic receptors in the autonomic ganglia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct agonism of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct agonism of M2 muscarinic receptors in the sinoatrial node

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in cardiac conduction tissue

explanation.summary: Atropine increases heart rate in arrhythmias by competitively inhibiting acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.
